entries.title: ACV and ARR
entries.one_line_definition: Average contract value per deal, and the annual recurring revenue the base produces.
entries.why_it_matters: They are the two numbers that describe the shape of a subscription business. ACV says what a customer is worth per deal; ARR says what the base is worth per year.
entries.body:
ACV is the average size of a single contract. ARR is the revenue the whole customer base produces in a year, treating everything as recurring.

Together they separate two growth stories that look identical from the outside. A company growing by adding large contracts is buying growth; one growing by compounding a stable base is building an asset.

## Worked example

A company has 200 customers:

    150 at $10,000/year   = 1,500,000
     40 at $40,000/year   = 1,600,000
     10 at $150,000/year  = 1,500,000
    ARR                   = 4,600,000
    ACV                   = 4,600,000 / 200 = 23,000

The ACV of $23,000 hides a base that is really three businesses. Ten customers produce a third of the revenue, so losing one is a $150,000 event. A company that does not know this will not notice the concentration risk until it bites.

## Watch for

- **ARR excludes one-time fees.** Setup, implementation, and services should be reported separately, or the recurring base looks healthier than it is.
- **Net new ARR is the growth number.** Total ARR rises even when existing customers downgrade, if new business is large enough to mask it.
- **ACV is a blend.** Report it by segment, because the average across segments is not a price anyone pays.
entries.formula: ARR = sum of all active contracts normalised to a year
entries.how_to_read: Read them together with churn. A high ARR with high churn is a leak; a modest ARR with near-zero churn is a compounding asset.

entries.title: Anchoring
entries.one_line_definition: The tendency for the first number mentioned in a discussion to pull every later number toward it.
entries.why_it_matters: It means the first offer often sets the outcome. A negotiation that starts at the wrong number spends the rest of its time recovering from it.
entries.body:
Anchoring is the cognitive bias where the first number in a discussion becomes the baseline for everything that follows. It operates even when the number is obviously arbitrary.

The commercial consequence is that the order of speaking matters. Whoever states a number first has set the range, and the other party's counter will be pulled toward it rather than toward the true value.

## Worked example

A supplier negotiation over an annual contract:

    Buyer speaks first:   "We were thinking $80,000."
    Supplier was prepared to accept $100,000. Final: $92,000.

    Supplier speaks first: "Our rate is $140,000."
    Buyer was prepared to pay $110,000. Final: $118,000.

The underlying value is the same in both cases. The first number shifted the settlement by roughly $20,000 in each direction — about 20% of the contract — with no change in the work.

## Watch for

- **Know your number before the meeting.** If you cannot state a well-supported figure, you will accept theirs.
- **A high anchor needs support.** An aggressive first offer with no reasoning behind it damages credibility. Anchor high and explain why.
- **Anchors work in both directions.** A salary candidate who names a range first shifts the offer; so does a customer who states a budget.
entries.statement: The first figure stated becomes the reference point for the whole discussion, and later adjustments are made from there rather than from the underlying value.
entries.evidence: In studies of negotiation, arbitrary first offers consistently shift final settlements in the direction of that offer, even when both parties know the number was random.
entries.failure_mode: Naming your price first out of politeness, or accepting the other party's anchor because it is the only number on the table.

entries.title: ARPU and ARPPU
entries.one_line_definition: Average revenue per user, and per paying user.
entries.why_it_matters: It separates two ways to grow revenue: adding customers, or earning more from the ones you have. Most businesses underestimate the second.
entries.body:
ARPU is revenue divided by users. ARPPU is revenue divided by *paying* users. The difference matters because the two move for different reasons.

ARPU rises when you sell more to existing customers or when the mix shifts toward bigger ones. ARPPU rises when each paying customer spends more. A falling ARPPU with a rising ARPU means you are acquiring many small customers, which usually means higher churn and lower lifetime value.

## Worked example

A company has 10,000 registered users and 2,000 paying ones. Monthly revenue is $60,000:

    ARPU  = 60,000 / 10,000 = $6.00
    ARPPU = 60,000 /  2,000 = $30.00

Now a price increase lifts revenue to $66,000 with the same user counts:

    ARPU  = $6.60   (+10%)
    ARPPU = $33.00  (+10%)

Both rose together, which is what a clean price increase looks like. If instead ARPU rose to $7.20 while ARPPU stayed at $30, the growth came from converting free users rather than from customers spending more — a different, and usually less durable, source.

## Watch for

- **Which denominator.** Reporting ARPU against paying users while comparing it to a competitor's ARPU against all users produces a meaningless comparison.
- **ARPU hides distribution.** A few very large customers can carry the average. Check the median.
- **See [ltv](#ltv).** ARPU is a period figure; LTV is the cumulative one. A rising ARPU with a falling LTV means customers are spending more but leaving sooner.
entries.formula: ARPU = total revenue / number of users
entries.how_to_read: Read ARPU and ARPPU together. A rising ARPU with a falling ARPPU means the mix is shifting toward smaller customers, which is a warning.

entries.title: Attribution
entries.one_line_definition: Deciding which touchpoint caused a conversion.
entries.why_it_matters: It decides where budget goes. Get it wrong and you cut the channel that created demand and keep the one that merely took credit.
entries.body:
Attribution is the answer to "which marketing caused this sale?" It is a modelling problem, not a measurement problem, because the customer's path is not observable end to end.

Every model is a simplification. Last-click gives all credit to the final touch. First-click gives it all to the first. Linear splits it evenly. Each produces a different budget, and none is correct.

## Worked example

A customer sees a podcast mention, Googles the category a week later, clicks a paid ad, and buys. Three models:

    Last-click:   paid search 100%, podcast 0%
    First-click:  podcast 100%, paid search 0%
    Linear:       33% each

Under last-click the podcast looks worthless and gets cancelled. Under first-click the paid search gets cancelled — and the customer now has no ad to click. Both decisions are wrong, and both are made from the same underlying behaviour.

## Watch for

- **State your model.** An attribution number without its model is uninterpretable, and two teams using different models will disagree about the same data.
- **Incrementality is the honest test.** Hold out a channel or a region and measure what sales disappear. Everything else is inference.
- **Do not over-invest in precision.** A roughly right model applied consistently beats a precise model applied once.
entries.how_to_read: Read any attribution number as a model, not a fact. Last-click is the most common model and the most misleading.

entries.title: The Balance Sheet
entries.one_line_definition: A snapshot of what a business owns and what it owes at a single moment.
entries.why_it_matters: It answers the question the income statement cannot: what would be left if everything were sold and every debt repaid today.
entries.body:
The balance sheet is a photograph, not a film. It lists assets (what the business owns), liabilities (what it owes), and equity (what belongs to the owners) at one instant, and the two sides always balance.

Its value is in the structure. Current assets against current liabilities tells you whether the business can pay its bills in the next year. Debt against equity tells you how much of the company is borrowed and how much is owned.

## Worked example

    Assets
      Cash                    200,000
      Accounts receivable     150,000
      Inventory               100,000
      Equipment               250,000
      Total                   700,000

    Liabilities
      Accounts payable        120,000
      Loan                    180,000
      Total                   300,000

    Equity                  =   400,000
    Total                   =   700,000

Current ratio = (200,000 + 150,000 + 100,000) / 120,000 = 3.75. The business can cover its short-term obligations comfortably. But equity of $400,000 against $180,000 of debt means it is financed mostly by its owners, which is conservative and slow.

## Watch for

- **It is a moment, not a trend.** A healthy balance sheet the day before a bad quarter is still a healthy balance sheet. Read it over time.
- **Inventory and receivables are not cash.** They are assets that must convert. A large receivables balance can hide a cash problem.
- **Off-balance-sheet items.** Leases, guarantees, and commitments may not appear as liabilities and still bind the business.
entries.formula: Assets = liabilities + equity
entries.how_to_read: Read it for solvency and structure, not performance. A profitable company can still have a balance sheet that is about to break.

entries.title: BATNA
entries.one_line_definition: Your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — what you will do if this deal does not happen.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the only source of real power in a negotiation. A strong alternative lets you walk away; without one, you are accepting terms rather than agreeing to them.
entries.body:
BATNA is what you do if the negotiation fails. It is the standard against which any offer should be measured, and it is the true source of negotiating power.

The common mistake is negotiating against your hopes rather than against your alternative. A customer offering $80,000 feels acceptable if you hoped for $70,000 — but if your alternative is doing nothing, $80,000 is the best outcome available and the customer knows it.

## Worked example

A company is choosing a supplier. Its BATNA is an in-house build costing $120,000 and three months.

    Supplier A offers $90,000        →  better than BATNA by $30,000. Acceptable.
    Supplier B offers $130,000       →  worse than BATNA by $10,000. Build in-house.
    Supplier C offers $85,000 but is unreliable  →  the risk may make the true cost exceed $120,000.

The BATNA is not a number to mention — it is a decision rule. Knowing it means the company can walk away from B without regret, which is exactly why it can afford to.

## Watch for

- **Improve your BATNA before negotiating.** A second quote, an in-house option, or a delay all strengthen your position more than any tactic at the table.
- **Do not reveal it.** Telling the other party your alternative hands them the ceiling of your flexibility.
- **Estimate theirs.** A supplier with no other customers has a weak BATNA and will concede more. Power is relative, not absolute.
entries.how_to_read: Read every negotiation by comparing the offer to your alternative, not to your ideal. A mediocre deal better than your alternative is worth taking.

entries.title: Cognitive Bias
entries.one_line_definition: A systematic error in judgment that comes from how the mind processes information, not from missing information.
entries.why_it_matters: It produces confident, wrong decisions that feel well-reasoned. Because the error is systematic, it cannot be removed by trying harder — only by changing the process.
entries.body:
A cognitive bias is a predictable way the mind reaches a wrong conclusion from correct information. Confirmation bias, sunk cost, anchoring, and survivorship bias are all examples, and all of them feel like clear thinking from the inside.

The practical point is that biases are not fixed by awareness. Knowing about confirmation bias does not stop you seeking confirming evidence. What works is process: requiring the opposing case, pre-committing to a decision rule, and separating the person who proposes from the person who decides.

## Worked example

A founder must decide whether to launch a second product line:

    Confirmation bias:  reads three success stories, ignores the twenty failures.
    Sunk cost:           "we've already spent $80,000 on it" — that money is gone either way.
    Anchoring:           the first revenue estimate of $500,000 frames every later revision.
    Survivorship:        the one comparable company that succeeded is the only one anyone can name.

Countermeasures: seek out the failures deliberately; decide on future costs and future returns only; have someone independent produce the first estimate; ask what the base rate is for companies in this position.

## Watch for

- **Awareness is not a defence.** The bias you can name is still operating. Process is the defence.
- **Bias is strongest where stakes are high and feedback is slow.** Exactly the conditions of a strategic decision.
- **Look for the decision you made fastest.** Slow, argued decisions are more likely to have been examined; instant ones are more likely to be bias wearing the costume of intuition.
entries.how_to_read: Read bias as a reason to distrust your own confidence, not as a reason to distrust data. The strongest signal is a decision you reached quickly and cannot argue against.

entries.title: Board Meeting
entries.one_line_definition: A checklist for running a board meeting that produces decisions instead of updates.
entries.why_it_matters: A board meeting is the most expensive two hours a company spends. Most of them are wasted.
entries.body:
A board meeting is a decision-making forum disguised as a reporting exercise.
Most founders treat it as the latter and are surprised when it produces no
decisions. The fix is to design the meeting around the decisions, not the data.

## Before the meeting

Send the deck a week ahead, with the narrative, not just the numbers. A board
that reads the deck in the meeting is a board that is not deciding. The meeting
should start with the assumption that everyone has read it, and spend its time on
the questions it raised.

## The agenda

Three items, in this order:

1. What changed since last time.
2. What decisions need to be made now.
3. What help you need from the board.

Item one is short. Item two is the meeting. Item three is why the board exists.

## The bad news

Put it first, not last. A board that hears bad news in the first five minutes
has time to help. A board that hears it in the last five minutes has time to
react. The reaction is not the same as the help.

## After the meeting

Send minutes within 48 hours, including the decisions and the owners. A meeting
that produces no written record produces no accountability, and a board that is
not accountable to its own decisions is a board that is performing.
entries.trigger: You are preparing for a board meeting, and need to make it useful rather than performative.
questions: What decisions need to be made, and by whom?
What does the board need to know that they do not already?
What are you not telling them?
What do you want them to do between now and the next meeting?
numbers_to_pull: Revenue and growth rate vs. plan
Burn rate and runway
Key metrics by segment
Hiring progress against plan
traps: Treating the meeting as a status update
Sending the deck the night before
Hiding bad news in the appendix
Asking for approval instead of advice

entries.title: Bootstrapping vs Venture Capital
entries.one_line_definition: Funding the business from its own revenue, or from outside investors in exchange for equity.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the decision that sets the ceiling on the company. Venture money buys speed at the cost of control and a permanent obligation to grow; bootstrapping buys control at the cost of speed.
entries.body:
Bootstrapping means growing from revenue. Venture capital means selling equity to buy growth faster than revenue allows. They are not better or worse; they are different instruments with different terms.

The real trade-off is not money. It is control and obligation. Venture money requires a return, which requires an exit, which constrains every later decision. Bootstrapping leaves the founders free and caps the speed.

## Worked example

A company needs $2,000,000 to reach its next stage:

    Bootstrapped path:
      Current revenue          $400,000/yr
      Contribution margin      70%  →  $280,000 available
      Time to raise $2,000,000  ≈ 7 years of retained profit
      Equity given up           0%

    Venture path:
      Raise $2,000,000         now
      Equity given up           20-25%
      Obligation                a return, which requires an exit in ~7 years
      Growth rate               constrained by the market, not by cash

If the market is large and the window is short, the venture path is the only one that can win it. If the market is modest and the business is profitable from month one, the venture path gives away control for speed the business does not need.

## Watch for

- **Venture money is a means, not a milestone.** Raising is not success; it is a loan against a future you now have to build.
- **Runway is the real cost.** See [runway](#runway). Venture funding extends it, which is valuable only if you use the time to become fundable again on better terms.
- **Bootstrapping has a ceiling.** Some markets cannot be served at a scale that supports the team, and no amount of patience changes that.
entries.when_to_use: When deciding how to fund the next stage, or when an investor offer arrives and you need to compare it against the alternative.
entries.when_not_to_use: To judge one path as superior. The right answer depends on the market size, the margin structure, and what the founders want to own.
steps: Estimate how much capital the plan requires and by when.
Estimate how much of that the business can generate itself.
Price the equity you would give up and the growth you would be forced into.
Compare the two futures, not the two amounts of money.
entries.limitations: The comparison is a forecast, and both paths carry risk the numbers cannot show — a startup that runs out of cash and a bootstrapped company that never reaches scale.

entries.title: Bottlenecks and Theory of Constraints
entries.one_line_definition: A system's output is limited by its single slowest step, so improving anything else does not increase output.
entries.why_it_matters: It redirects effort from the work that feels productive to the work that actually moves the number. Most improvement programmes optimise the wrong step.
entries.body:
The Theory of Constraints says a system's throughput is capped by one step. Everything upstream of it produces faster than it can consume; everything downstream starves.

The discipline is a loop: find the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, then elevate it. When the constraint moves, start again. The mistake is trying to optimise all steps at once, which improves cost and local efficiency while leaving output unchanged.

## Worked example

A software release pipeline:

    Commit       200/day
    Build        180/day
    Test          40/day   ← constraint
    Deploy       100/day

The constraint is testing. The team hires two more developers, and commit rate rises to 260/day. Test still does 40/day, so the backlog grows, and releases per day do not change. The hire added cost and queue.

Elevating testing to 80/day by adding a test engineer doubles output. Now build at 180 becomes the constraint, and the loop restarts.

## Watch for

- **The constraint is not always where the backlog is largest.** Look for the step with the least spare capacity relative to demand.
- **Subordinating is the hard part.** It means deliberately leaving other steps under-utilised, which feels wrong to every manager.
- **Constraints move.** An improvement that does not move the constraint did not improve the system, even if it improved a metric.
entries.statement: Every system has exactly one constraint at a time. Improve it and the constraint moves. Improve anything else and nothing changes.
entries.evidence: In every observed production and service system, raising capacity at a non-constraining step increased work-in-progress and cost without increasing completed output.
entries.failure_mode: Spreading improvement effort evenly across all steps because it feels fair, and being surprised that throughput does not move.

entries.title: Brand
entries.one_line_definition: The expectation a customer holds about what you will do, built from every interaction.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the reason a customer chooses you before comparing. A strong brand lowers acquisition cost and raises the price the market will pay.
entries.body:
A brand is what a customer expects before they experience the product. It is accumulated, not declared: every support reply, every late shipment, every price change adds to it or subtracts from it.

Its commercial value is concrete. A trusted brand converts better at the same price, survives a mistake that would kill an unknown one, and can charge more because the risk of choosing it feels lower.

## Worked example

Two suppliers sell an identical component at $10. One is well known, the other unknown:

    Known brand:   converts 8% of enquiries, supports $12 price
    Unknown brand: converts 3%, supports $10 price

On 1,000 enquiries the known brand makes 80 sales at $12 = $960; the unknown makes 30 at $10 = $300. The product is identical. The brand is worth more than three times the revenue, and it was built from reliability over years, not from a redesign.

## Watch for

- **Brand is a liability when broken.** A promise the product does not keep turns the brand against you, because it raises expectations you then miss.
- **Branding is not the brand.** A new identity cannot create trust; it can only express trust that already exists.
- **Brand compounds slowly and erodes fast.** One bad quarter can undo two years of consistency, which is why it is an operational commitment, not a campaign.
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a promise kept, not as a logo or a tone of voice. The assets are the residue of the behaviour.

entries.title: Break-even
entries.one_line_definition: The point where revenue exactly covers all costs, so profit is zero.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the first number that tells you whether the business model works at all, before growth or market share enters the picture.
entries.body:
Break-even is where total revenue equals total cost. It is the smallest volume at which the business stops losing money on its own operations.

It matters because it separates "we need more customers" from "the model is wrong." A company far below break-even can fix itself with growth. A company that cannot reach break-even at any realistic volume has a pricing or cost problem, and no amount of marketing fixes that.

## Worked example

A coffee cart has fixed costs of $3,000 a month. Each coffee sells for $4 and costs $1 to make:

    Contribution margin per unit = 4 - 1 = 3
    Break-even = 3,000 / 3 = 1,000 coffees a month

That is about 33 coffees a day. If the cart sells 600 a month it loses $1,200; at 1,500 it makes $1,500. The break-even number is the line between those two futures.

Now raise the price to $5 with the same cost: contribution margin becomes $4 and break-even falls to 750 coffees. The same cart, the same costs, a 25% smaller target.

## Watch for

- **Fixed costs move.** Rent, salaries, and tooling are decisions. Break-even moves when they do.
- **Contribution margin, not gross margin.** Forgetting variable selling costs makes break-even look closer than it is.
- **Break-even is not cash flow.** You can be above break-even on paper and still run out of cash if customers pay slowly.
entries.formula: Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution margin per unit
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a volume and a date. Below break-even every sale loses money; above it every sale funds profit.

entries.title: Burn Rate
entries.one_line_definition: How fast a company spends more cash than it brings in.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the countdown timer on the business. Every strategic decision is bounded by how many months of burn remain.
entries.body:
Burn rate is net cash outflow per month: what you spent minus what you earned. A company with $300,000 of costs and $100,000 of revenue has a burn rate of $200,000.

The number that matters is not the burn itself but the ratio of cash to burn — that is [runway](#runway). Burn tells you the speed; runway tells you the time.

## Worked example

A startup has $1,200,000 in the bank.

- Month 1-3: costs $250,000, revenue $50,000 → burn $200,000/month
- Month 4-6: costs $280,000, revenue $80,000 → burn $200,000/month
- Month 7: hires two engineers, costs $340,000, revenue $90,000 → burn $250,000/month

    Average burn over 7 months = (200k*6 + 250k) / 7 = 207,143

At $207,000 a month, $1,200,000 lasts about 5.8 months. If the next fundraise takes four months, the company is fine. If it takes eight, it is not — and the decision to hire was made in month 7 without knowing that.

## Watch for

- **Gross vs net burn.** Gross burn is total spend; net burn subtracts revenue. Investors ask for both because they behave very differently.
- **Burn is a lagging indicator.** By the time the number is bad, the decisions that caused it are months old.
- **See [runway](#runway)** — the two are useless apart.
entries.formula: Burn rate = cash spent - cash earned, per month
entries.how_to_read: Read it as months, not dollars. A $200,000 monthly burn is a different business at $40,000 of cash than at $2,000,000.

entries.title: Customer Acquisition Cost
entries.one_line_definition: What you spend to acquire one paying customer.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the denominator of every growth decision. Growth at a CAC above what a customer pays back is a machine for converting cash into churn.
entries.body:
Customer acquisition cost is the total cost of sales and marketing divided by
the number of customers that effort produced. It is the price of growth.

The trap is that it is almost always reported blended — all spend over all
customers — and a blended number can hide a broken channel inside a healthy
average. Two channels can each be individually bad and jointly look acceptable.
The useful form is per channel, per cohort, over time.

## Worked example

In one quarter a company spends:

- Paid ads: $120,000 → 400 customers
- Content and SEO: $60,000 → 100 customers
- Sales team (2 reps): $180,000 → 300 customers

    Blended CAC = (120,000 + 60,000 + 180,000) / 800 = $450

    Per channel:  ads $300   |   content $600   |   sales $600

The blended number suggests $450. The real picture: ads are the only channel
under $450, and content — the cheapest to scale — costs $600. If the customer
pays back $500, content and sales are losing money while ads barely break even.
That conclusion is invisible in the blended figure.

## Watch for

- **Attribution inflates CAC in your favour.** Last-click credit will hand the
  sale to the cheapest channel and make every expensive one look worse, or
  vice versa. Say which model you are using, because it changes the number.
- **CAC is not payback.** A customer acquired for $450 who pays back in three
  months is a different business from one who takes three years. Pair this with
  [contribution-margin](#contribution-margin) and payback period.
- **See [roas](#roas)** for the same trade-off expressed as revenue per dollar
  spent rather than cost per customer.
entries.formula: CAC = total acquisition spend / new customers acquired
entries.how_to_read: Blended CAC hides your best and worst channels. Read it per channel, and always against payback period.

entries.title: CAC Spike
entries.one_line_definition: A checklist for diagnosing and fixing a sudden rise in customer acquisition cost.
entries.why_it_matters: CAC is the price you pay for growth. A spike means the market got more expensive or you got less efficient, and the difference matters.
entries.body:
A CAC spike is a symptom with several possible diseases. The first move is to
split it, because the split tells you which one you have and the aggregate tells
you nothing.

## Split by channel

CAC is an average, and averages hide. If one channel spiked while the others
held, the problem is that channel. If every channel moved together, the problem
is your conversion rate, your pricing, or your market, and no channel fix will
solve it.

## Split conversion from cost

A rising CAC can come from traffic getting more expensive, conversion getting
worse, or both. They have different causes and different fixes. Pull cost per
click and conversion rate separately before you decide what to do.

## The timeline

Plot CAC against every change in the last 60 days: creative refreshes, landing
page changes, bid strategy changes, competitor launches. The spike usually lines
up with one of them. If it does not, check seasonality and auction dynamics
before concluding it is mysterious.

## The response

Do not cut spend across the board. Cut the channel that moved, fix the
conversion problem, and re-measure. Cutting everything treats a local problem
as a global one and loses the channels that were working.
entries.trigger: Your customer acquisition cost has risen sharply, and you need to find the cause and decide the response.
questions: Which channel got more expensive?
Did conversion drop, or did traffic cost more?
Is the spike in one segment or across the board?
Did a competitor enter the auction?
numbers_to_pull: CAC by channel, trailing 90 days
Cost per click and conversion rate by channel
CAC by segment and cohort
LTV by channel to check whether the economics still hold
traps: Blaming the channel when the landing page broke
Cutting spend before diagnosing
Averaging CAC across channels and missing the one that moved
Ignoring that LTV may have moved too

entries.title: Cap Table
entries.one_line_definition: The record of who owns what percentage of the company, and on what terms.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the document that decides who controls the company and who receives the value when there is a return. Small errors early become very expensive later.
entries.body:
The capitalisation table lists every holder of equity and their share. It starts simple — two founders, 50/50 — and grows complicated with every grant, every round, and every early agreement made on a handshake.

The reason it matters is that the table determines control. A founder who has sold 60% across rounds may still run the company day to day, but no longer decides its fate.

## Worked example

    Holder                    Shares     Percentage
    Founder A                  600,000       54.5%
    Founder B                  300,000       27.3%
    Option pool               150,000       13.6%
    Angel investor              50,000        4.5%
    Total                    1,100,000      100.0%

Now a seed round issues 200,000 new shares to an investor:

    Total shares             1,300,000
    Founder A                  600,000  →  46.2%
    Investor                   200,000  →  15.4%

Founder A's stake fell from 54.5% to 46.2% without selling anything. That is dilution, and it is why the size of the option pool and the valuation of each round are worth more argument than they usually receive.

## Watch for

- **Handshake equity is a cap-table problem waiting.** A co-founder who leaves at month three with unvested shares still holds them. Vest everything.
- **The option pool dilutes you, not the investor.** It is created before the round and paid for by existing holders, which founders often discover only after signing.
- **Model the next two rounds before signing this one.** The terms that look fine now can leave you without control by the round after.
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a set of claims, not a list of names. What matters is the percentage, the liquidation preference, and whether the shares are vested.

entries.title: The Cash Flow Statement
entries.one_line_definition: Where the cash actually came from and where it went, over a period.
entries.why_it_matters: Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. Businesses do not fail because they are unprofitable — they fail because they run out of cash.
entries.body:
The cash flow statement reconciles the gap between profit and cash. It explains why a company with $100,000 of profit can still have $20,000 less in the bank than it started with.

The three sections answer different questions. Operating cash flow asks whether the core business generates cash. Investing cash flow asks where that cash is being put to work. Financing cash flow asks who is funding the gap.

## Worked example

    Operating activities
      Net income                    100,000
      Depreciation                  + 20,000
      Increase in receivables       - 60,000
      Increase in payables          + 15,000
      Operating cash flow           = 75,000

    Investing activities
      Equipment purchase            - 40,000

    Financing activities
      Loan repayment                - 30,000
      Owner draw                    - 25,000

    Net change in cash             = -20,000

The company made $100,000 and ended with $20,000 less cash. The reason is in the receivables line: $60,000 of the profit has not been collected yet.

## Watch for

- **Positive operating cash flow is the goal.** A business that must keep raising money to fund operations is renting its survival.
- **Growth consumes cash.** More sales means more inventory and more receivables before the cash returns. Fast growth and a cash shortfall are the same event.
- **Depreciation is added back.** It reduced profit but not cash. Forgetting this is the most common way to misread the statement.
entries.formula: Net cash flow = cash in from operations + investing + financing
entries.how_to_read: Read it as three sections in order: operations, investing, financing. The first tells you if the business works; the other two tell you how it is funded.

entries.title: Channel Economics
entries.one_line_definition: The cost, volume, and quality of customers each acquisition route produces.
entries.why_it_matters: Two channels can deliver the same number of customers at wildly different cost and lifetime value. The channel is a business decision, not a marketing one.
entries.body:
Channel economics is the discipline of comparing acquisition routes on cost *and* customer quality. Cost per acquisition alone is misleading, because a cheap channel can deliver customers who leave immediately.

The comparison that matters is CAC against the lifetime value that channel produces. A channel with high cost and high value beats a channel with low cost and low value.

## Worked example

    Channel        CAC     Avg LTV   LTV/CAC   Verdict
    Paid search    $300     $900      3.0x    keep
    Paid social    $180     $300      1.7x    fix or cut
    Content/SEO    $120   $1,200      10.0x   scale
    Referral        $80   $1,000      12.5x   scale hard

Paid social looks affordable at $180 but its customers are worth $300 — barely viable. Content looks expensive to produce but delivers the best customers at the lowest effective cost. Referral is the standout and usually the most neglected.

## Watch for

- **Attribution corrupts the comparison.** See [attribution](#attribution) — the channel credited with a sale is often not the channel that caused it.
- **Channels saturate.** Doubling spend on a working channel usually raises its cost. The curve matters, not the point.
- **Channel fit is strategic.** A channel that reaches your segment is worth more than a cheap one that does not.
entries.when_to_use: When deciding where to spend acquisition budget, and when a channel's cost rises.
entries.when_not_to_use: When you have no data on a channel yet — test small before committing.
steps: List every route to a customer.
Measure cost per acquisition for each.
Measure the lifetime value each channel's customers produce.
Compare the ratio, not the cost alone.
entries.limitations: Channel economics shift. A channel that works at one price point or one scale often stops working at another.

entries.title: Churn Rate
entries.one_line_definition: The share of customers who stop using the product in a period.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the leak in the bucket. Growth fills the bucket; churn empties it. A leak you cannot measure is a leak you cannot fix.
entries.body:
Churn is the percentage of customers who leave in a period. It is the single most important retention metric because it compounds: a small monthly rate removes a large share of the base over a year.

Its power is in combination with growth. A company growing 10% a month with 5% churn is adding 5% net. The same company at 2% churn is adding 8% net — a 60% faster compounding rate from a change most founders treat as a support problem.

## Worked example

A company starts the month with 1,000 customers and loses 40:

    Monthly churn = 40 / 1,000 = 4%

Over a year, 4% monthly churn removes a startling share of the base. The average customer lifetime is roughly 1 / 0.04 = 25 months. Now suppose churn falls to 2%:

    Average lifetime = 1 / 0.02 = 50 months

The lifetime doubled. With a contribution margin of $35 a month, LTV goes from $875 to $1,750 — without acquiring a single new customer.

## Watch for

- **Gross vs net churn.** Gross churn ignores the customers who upgrade. Net churn counts expansion revenue as a reduction, which can make a bad retention picture look stable.
- **Revenue churn is not customer churn.** Losing one large customer can exceed losing many small ones. Track both.
- **Churn has causes that differ.** Involuntary churn (failed payments) is a fixable operational problem; voluntary churn is a product problem. Treat them separately.
entries.formula: Churn = customers lost in period / customers at start of period
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a rate per month for subscriptions and per period for one-time products. Compare it to your growth rate, not to an industry average.

entries.title: Churn Spike
entries.one_line_definition: A checklist for diagnosing and responding to a sudden rise in churn.
entries.why_it_matters: Churn is the leak in the bucket. A spike is a signal, not a mystery, if you know where to look.
entries.body:
A churn spike is a question, not a verdict. The first move is to stop
panicking and start segmenting, because the cause is almost always visible in
the breakdown and invisible in the average.

## Segment first

Split churn by cohort, plan, channel, and tenure. A spike that hits only new
customers points to onboarding or acquisition quality. A spike that hits
established customers points to a product change, a competitor, or a pricing
shift. The answer is in the split; the aggregate tells you nothing.

## Separate voluntary from involuntary

Involuntary churn — failed payments, expired cards — is the cheapest to fix and
the most commonly ignored. Dunning, retry logic, and card-update prompts can
recover a meaningful share of it. Fix this before touching the product.

## The timeline

Plot churn against every change in the last 60 days: releases, price changes,
marketing campaigns, competitor launches. The spike usually lines up with one
of them. If it does not, look at seasonality and acquisition mix before
concluding it is mysterious.

## The response

Do not discount. A discount retains the customer you have and trains them to
threaten to leave. Fix the cause, communicate the fix, and let the data tell
you whether it worked.
entries.trigger: Your churn rate has risen sharply, and you need to find the cause and decide the response.
questions: When did it start, and what changed?
Which cohort churned — new or established?
Is it voluntary or involuntary?
Did a competitor ship something?
numbers_to_pull: Churn rate by cohort and acquisition month
Churn rate by plan and channel
Failed payment rate (involuntary churn)
NPS or support ticket volume, pre and post
traps: Averaging churn across cohorts and missing the spike
Treating all churn as a product problem
Offering discounts before diagnosing
Ignoring involuntary churn, which is the cheapest to fix

entries.title: Cost of Goods Sold
entries.one_line_definition: What it costs to produce the goods or services you sold.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the first deduction from revenue, and the line that decides whether your margin is a choice or a surprise.
entries.body:
Cost of goods sold is the cost of producing what you sold, and nothing else. It
includes materials, direct labour, and the overhead you can attribute to
production. It excludes rent for the office, sales salaries, and the software
your engineers use — those are operating expenses, and mixing them in is the
most common way to make a healthy business look broken.

The distinction matters because it decides what you compare. COGS against
revenue tells you the margin you earn by existing. Operating expenses against
gross margin tells you whether your business model scales or just your to-do
list.

## Worked example

A reseller reports:

- Revenue: $1,000,000
- Beginning inventory: $50,000
- Purchases during the year: $400,000
- Ending inventory: $80,000

    COGS = 50,000 + 400,000 - 80,000 = 370,000
    Gross margin = 1,000,000 - 370,000 = 630,000  (63%)

Now suppose next year revenue is flat at $1,000,000 but COGS rises to $500,000.
Gross margin falls to 50%. Revenue did not move; the business got worse. That is
the signal this term exists to give you, and it is invisible if you only read
revenue.

## Watch for

- **Capitalising what should be expensed.** Software and rent are not COGS.
  Putting them there inflates gross margin and hides a cash problem.
- **Inventory changes masking a price cut.** A falling ending inventory with
  flat purchases usually means you sold down stock, not that you got cheaper.
- **Comparing COGS across business models.** A manufacturer's COGS is a
  different animal from a SaaS company's, where COGS is hosting and support.
entries.formula: COGS = beginning inventory + purchases - ending inventory
entries.how_to_read: Compare COGS to revenue, never to itself. Rising COGS with flat pricing is margin compression, not growth.

entries.title: Cohort Analysis
entries.one_line_definition: Tracking groups of customers by when they arrived, and comparing how each group behaves over time.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the only way to see whether the business is actually improving. Aggregate metrics rise even when every group of customers is getting worse.
entries.body:
Cohort analysis groups customers by when they arrived and follows each group separately. It replaces a single average with a set of comparable histories.

The reason it matters is that aggregates lie. A company can show rising retention while every individual cohort is decaying, because a large new cohort lifts the average. Cohort analysis removes that illusion by comparing like with like.

## Worked example

    Retention by acquisition month

                  Month 1   Month 3   Month 6   Month 12
    Jan cohort      82%       58%       44%       38%
    Feb cohort      80%       55%       41%       35%
    Mar cohort      79%       57%       43%        -
    Apr cohort      81%       54%        -         -

Reading across month 3, every cohort sits at 54–58%. Reading down the January column, that cohort decayed steadily. The flatness across cohorts says the product's retention is stable; the slope down each column says it is not improving. Both facts matter, and neither appears in an aggregate retention number.

## Watch for

- **Compare at the same age.** A January cohort at month 12 and an April cohort at month 3 are not comparable. Align by age, not by calendar.
- **Small cohorts are noise.** Below a few hundred, a handful of customers swings the percentage wildly.
- **Cohort quality changes with acquisition.** If March came from a new channel, its cohort may differ for reasons that have nothing to do with the product.
entries.when_to_use: Anytime a retention, revenue, or lifetime-value number looks wrong, or whenever you change pricing, onboarding, or targeting.
entries.when_not_to_use: When you have fewer than a few hundred customers per cohort — the percentages become noise.
steps: Group customers by acquisition month.
Compute the metric for each group at each age (month 1, 2, 3...).
Read down a column to see how one cohort ages.
Read across a row to see how newer cohorts compare at the same age.
entries.limitations: Cohorts need volume to be meaningful, and they describe the past. A cohort that looks healthy today tells you nothing about the cohort arriving next month.

entries.title: Competitive Advantage
entries.one_line_definition: A difference you can sustain that allows you to create more value than rivals.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the only source of durable profit. Everything else — effort, quality, speed — is available to everyone and gets competed away.
entries.body:
Competitive advantage is a position that lets you earn more than your rivals for the same effort. The word "sustain" is the whole concept: a lead is an advantage you have not yet converted.

The distinction between better and different is the practical core. Being better is a race anyone can join, and it ends in a price war. Being different changes the comparison the customer makes, so the race is not run at all.

## Worked example

Two accountants serve small businesses in the same town:

    A. "We are accurate and affordable."  — every accountant claims this. No comparison is possible, so price decides.
    B. "We specialise in restaurants, and we know your margin structure."  — the restaurant owner compares B to no one.

B is not better. B is different, and the difference is worth more to one specific buyer. That is an advantage, because it cannot be copied by a generalist without giving up their own generalist customers.

## Watch for

- **Advantage needs a customer.** A difference nobody values is a cost, not an advantage.
- **Advantage erodes.** Competitors copy, markets shift, and technology changes the basis of competition. Treat it as a depreciating asset.
- **Saying it is not having it.** "We have great people" and "we move fast" are not advantages — they are claims every competitor makes.
entries.statement: Advantage is not being better. It is being different in a way that matters to a specific customer and cannot be easily copied.
entries.evidence: Industries with many undifferentiated competitors show margins near cost. Industries where one firm holds a structural position show sustained excess returns.
entries.failure_mode: Confusing a temporary lead with an advantage, and spending the lead on growth instead of converting it into a moat.

entries.title: Contracts and Negotiation Basics
entries.one_line_definition: The written agreement that fixes what each party must do, and what happens if they do not.
entries.why_it_matters: It converts a handshake into something enforceable. Most business disputes are not about bad faith; they are about two parties remembering the same conversation differently.
entries.body:
A contract is a record of an agreement that a court can enforce. Its real value is not that it makes people behave — it is that it states, in advance, what happens when they do not.

The clauses that decide the outcome of a dispute are rarely the price. They are liability caps, termination rights, and who owns what if the relationship ends.

## Worked example

A development agency signs a client. Four clauses matter more than the fee:

    Liability cap      "Our total liability is limited to the fees paid."
                       Without it, a bug could expose the agency to the client's whole loss.

    Termination        "Either party may terminate on 30 days' notice."
                       Without it, the agency can be locked into an unhappy client for years.

    IP assignment      "Work product transfers on full payment."
                       Without it, the client owns nothing until they have paid — and vice versa.

    Payment terms      "Net 30, with a 1.5% monthly late fee."
                       Without it, the agency finances the client.

A contract with a generous fee and none of these clauses is worse than one with a lower fee and all of them.

## Watch for

- **The contract is the relationship.** If you cannot agree on the failure terms, the relationship is already in trouble.
- **Read the termination clause first.** It tells you how you get out, which is the question you will ask when things go wrong.
- **Do not sign under pressure.** A deadline imposed by the other side is a reason to read more carefully, not less.
entries.how_to_read: Read a contract for what happens on failure, not for what happens on success. The clauses that matter are termination, liability, and who bears the risk.

entries.title: Contribution Margin
entries.one_line_definition: Revenue left over after every cost that varies with the sale.
entries.why_it_matters: It answers the only question a new offer can be judged on: does each additional sale leave money behind, or cost money?
entries.body:
Contribution margin is gross margin taken one step further. Gross margin
subtracts the cost of producing the thing; contribution margin also subtracts
everything else that changes when you make one more sale — payment processing,
sales commission, shipping, a salesperson's time, ad spend attributed to the
sale.

It is the number that decides whether an offer is worth making. Gross margin
can be healthy while contribution margin is negative, because the sale costs
more to acquire and fulfil than it brings in. That is a profitable-looking
company quietly paying customers to arrive.

## Worked example

An online course sells for $200. Per sale:

- Payment processing: $6
- Affiliate commission: $40
- Hosting and support: $10
- Ad spend attributed to the sale: $90

    Contribution margin = 200 - 6 - 40 - 10 - 90 = $54 per sale

Each sale puts $54 toward fixed costs. If the course has $10,000 in fixed
costs, you need 186 sales to break even, and every sale after that is $54 of
profit.

Now raise the ad spend to $160 per sale: contribution margin becomes -$16. You
are now losing $16 every time someone buys. Doubling traffic doubles the
losses. That is the trap this term exists to catch.

## Watch for

- **Ad spend belongs here, not in operating expenses.** If you exclude
  acquisition cost you get a number that looks like contribution margin but
  behaves like gross margin.
- **It is per unit, and units differ.** A $54 contribution on a $200 course is
  not the same as $54 on a $2,000 course. Compare the percentage too.
- **See [roas](#roas) for the ratio view** of the same trade-off: how much you
  spend to earn a dollar of revenue.
entries.formula: Contribution margin per unit = price - variable cost per unit
entries.how_to_read: If it is negative, no amount of volume saves you. If it is positive, every sale funds some fixed cost.

entries.title: Delegation
entries.one_line_definition: Handing over both the task and the authority needed to complete it, while keeping the outcome yours.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the only mechanism by which a founder's capacity grows. Without it, the business is capped at one person's working hours.
entries.body:
Delegation is giving someone else a result to own, with the authority to decide how to achieve it. The two parts are inseparable, and most delegation fails on the second.

The reason it is hard is that the founder's judgment is the business's advantage, and handing it over feels like giving that up. But judgment applied to one task is a bottleneck, and the goal is to multiply it by building judgment in other people.

## Worked example

A founder handles every customer refund personally. Delegating well:

    Task:    "Approve refunds up to $200."
    Bad:     "Let me know about any refund request and I'll decide."
    Good:    "Refund up to $200 without asking me. Above $200, bring me the case. Review the pattern monthly with me."

The bad version delegates the work and keeps the decision — so the founder is still the constraint, and now also reviews every request. The good version delegates the decision within a boundary, keeps the founder informed at a level they can act on, and creates a person who learns to judge.

## Watch for

- **Delegation needs a boundary.** Authority without limits is abdication, and the failure mode is a decision the founder would never have made.
- **You cannot delegate what you cannot define.** If you cannot state the outcome, the other person cannot own it.
- **Delegation is an investment with a return lag.** The first attempt usually takes longer than doing it yourself. That is the cost of building capacity, not evidence the approach failed.
entries.statement: Delegation without authority is not delegation; it is assignment. The person doing the work must be able to make the decisions that affect the outcome.
entries.evidence: Founders who delegate decisions, not just tasks, grow revenue faster and report lower burnout; those who retain every decision cap the organisation at their own capacity.
entries.failure_mode: Delegating the task and withholding the authority, then redoing the work when it is done differently than you would have done it.

entries.title: Dilution and Ownership
entries.one_line_definition: The reduction in each shareholder's percentage ownership caused by issuing new shares.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the true cost of outside money. A founder's stake falls with every round whether or not they sell anything, and the fall is permanent.
entries.body:
Dilution is what happens to your percentage when new shares are issued. It is not the same as losing money — your share of a much larger company can be worth far more — but it is permanent and it compounds.

The distinction founders miss is between percentage and value. Giving away 20% feels like losing a fifth of the company. If the capital turns a $5,000,000 company into a $25,000,000 one, the founder's 80% of $25,000,000 is worth far more than 100% of $5,000,000.

## Worked example

A founder holds 1,000,000 of 1,000,000 shares — 100%.

    Round 1: 250,000 new shares
      Total 1,250,000 → founder holds 80.0%

    Round 2: 500,000 new shares
      Total 1,750,000 → founder holds 57.1%

    Round 3: 500,000 new shares
      Total 2,250,000 → founder holds 44.4%

Three rounds took the stake from 100% to 44.4%. If the company is now worth $40,000,000, that stake is $17,760,000 — against $5,000,000 for the whole company at the start. The percentage fell by more than half and the value rose more than three times.

## Watch for

- **Dilution is decided before the round, not during.** The option pool and the valuation are set at term-sheet stage.
- **Model to the exit, not to the next round.** A stake that looks thin at round three may still be the largest single holding.
- **Founders dilute twice.** Once through investment and once through hiring — the option pool comes out of existing holders' shares.
entries.formula: New ownership % = existing shares / total shares after the round
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a price, not a loss. Dilution is the cost of capital, and the question is whether the capital buys more value than the percentage given up.

entries.title: Entity Types
entries.one_line_definition: The legal form a business takes, which decides who can be sued, who pays tax, and who owns what.
entries.why_it_matters: It is a permanent decision made cheaply at the start and expensively later. The wrong form can make fundraising impossible or put personal assets at risk.
entries.body:
An entity type is the legal container the business operates inside. The common choices are sole proprietorship, LLC, and corporation, and they differ mainly in liability and taxation.

The two questions that decide it are: can a customer or creditor reach your personal assets, and does the business pay tax separately from you? Everything else is detail.

## Worked example

    Type             Liability         Tax              Can raise equity
    Sole trader      Personal assets   Through you      No
    LLC              Protected         Through you      Awkward
    C-corp           Protected         Business + you   Yes, cleanly

A freelance designer with no debt and no partners may be fine as a sole trader — simple, cheap, and the liability risk is low. A software company with outside investors must be a C-corp, because investors need shares and the liability protection. Choosing the sole trader form and then trying to raise money means converting later, which costs legal fees and delays the round.

## Watch for

- **Entity choice interacts with funding.** See [cap-table](#cap-table). Investors cannot easily buy into an LLC, and converting later is expensive.
- **The cheapest form is not the best form.** A sole trader pays less to set up and can be personally bankrupted by a contract dispute.
- **It varies by jurisdiction.** The names and rules differ by country and state. Get local advice; this entry describes the pattern, not your jurisdiction's law.
entries.how_to_read: Read it by liability and by tax, not by name. The differences that matter are whether your personal assets are exposed and how profits are taxed.

entries.title: Evaluating a Hire
entries.one_line_definition: A checklist for deciding whether to hire, and whether to hire this person.
entries.why_it_matters: A bad hire costs six months and a team's morale. A good hire is still expensive, but it compounds.
entries.body:
Hiring is a decision to spend a large amount of money on a bet about a person.
The bet is worth making only when the person will do something specific that
creates more value than they cost, and when you can tell whether they are doing
it.

## The role

Before you look at candidates, write down what the person will produce in their
first 90 days. Not "lead the team" or "own the function" — those are titles.
Write the deliverables. If you cannot, the role is not real yet, and hiring
will not make it real.

## The candidate

A resume is a story the candidate tells about themselves. A work sample is
evidence. Prefer the second. Give them a real problem from your business, with
real constraints, and watch how they think. The interview tells you how they
talk; the sample tells you how they work.

## The reference

References given by the candidate are marketing. References you find yourself
are signal. Ask the reference what the candidate was like on their worst day, and
listen for the pause before the answer.

## The decision

Hire when the cost of not hiring is higher than the cost of hiring, and when you
have a specific answer to "what will change." A hire made to relieve pressure
relieves it briefly and creates a permanent cost. A hire made to create value
compounds.
entries.trigger: You are considering a hire, and need to decide whether the role is real and whether this candidate is the right person for it.
questions: What is this person going to do that is not being done now?
Is the role a gap or a luxury?
What would change if you did not hire?
Can you describe what great looks like in 90 days?
numbers_to_pull: Revenue per employee, current and projected
The cost of the hire against the runway
Time to productivity for the last three hires
Output of the team the hire would join
traps: Hiring to relieve pressure rather than to create value
Confusing culture fit with comfort
Skipping the work sample
Hiring for the company you want to be, not the one you are

entries.title: Porter's Five Forces
entries.one_line_definition: Five sources of competitive pressure that together determine how profitable an industry can be.
entries.why_it_matters: It stops you judging a business by its growth and forces you to ask whether the industry structure allows profit at all.
entries.body:
Five Forces asks whether an industry is structurally capable of producing profit. The five pressures are new entrants, supplier power, buyer power, substitutes, and rivalry.

The point is that a great company in a bad industry earns less than an average company in a good one. Structure dominates execution, which is why the framework is worth running before committing years to a market.

## Worked example

A specialty coffee roaster:

    New entrants        Low barrier — a roaster costs little to start. High pressure.
    Suppliers           Commodity beans, many sources. Low pressure.
    Buyers              Cafes and consumers, many choices. High pressure.
    Substitutes         Instant, tea, energy drinks. High pressure.
    Rivalry             Many roasters, undifferentiated. High pressure.

Four of five forces are adverse. The industry can contain good companies, but it will not produce structural margin, so profit depends on execution and branding rather than position. Compare a patent-protected drug: one force (new entrants) is blocked by regulation and the economics invert.

## Watch for

- **Define the industry tightly.** "Food" and "specialty coffee for offices" have completely different force profiles.
- **Forces change.** Buyer power rose sharply for many suppliers once procurement software made comparison trivial.
- **A favourable structure is not a strategy.** It tells you where to look, not what to build.
entries.when_to_use: Before entering a market, or when margins are falling and you need to know whether the cause is you or the structure.
entries.when_not_to_use: To evaluate a single company's execution — the framework describes industries, not firms.
steps: Assess the threat of new entrants.
Assess the power of suppliers.
Assess the power of buyers.
Assess the threat of substitutes.
Assess the intensity of rivalry.
Judge whether the combined pressure leaves room for margin.
entries.limitations: It is a static snapshot of an industry and was written before platform business models. It understates network effects and ecosystem lock-in.

entries.title: Framing
entries.one_line_definition: The way a proposal is presented, which changes what the other party hears without changing the substance.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the difference between the same offer being accepted and rejected. People respond to how a number sits relative to a reference point, not to the number itself.
entries.body:
Framing is the effect of context on a decision. The same price described as a discount from a higher number feels like a gain; described as a premium over a lower one, it feels like a loss.

It matters commercially because most negotiations are not about the number but about the reference point the number is measured against. Whoever sets that reference point usually wins the argument.

## Worked example

A freelancer quoting $4,000 for a project:

    Frame A:  "The project is $4,000."                    — no reference. The client compares it to their budget.
    Frame B:  "A full rebuild is $9,000. This is $4,000." — the client compares it to $9,000 and sees a saving.
    Frame C:  "This is $4,000, or $3,200 if we start this month." — the client compares two options and picks.

The work and the price are identical in all three. B anchors a higher number; C reframes the choice as a decision between two gains rather than a cost. Neither is dishonest, and both change the outcome.

## Watch for

- **Someone is always framing you.** A supplier's "our standard rate" is a frame. Ask what the alternatives are before accepting the reference point.
- **Framing is not lying.** Omitting a relevant comparison is not deception; it is presentation. Know the difference and stay on the right side of it.
- **The strongest frame is the true one.** A frame that collapses under one question costs you the relationship.
entries.how_to_read: Read every offer as a frame, not a fact. Ask what reference point it is being compared against, and who chose that reference.

entries.title: The Fundraising Process
entries.one_line_definition: The sequence of finding, pitching, and closing investors, from first outreach to money in the bank.
entries.why_it_matters: It is a sales process with a long cycle and a low close rate, and treating it as anything else is how companies run out of money while raising.
entries.body:
Fundraising is a process with a long cycle and a binary outcome, and the two together are what make it dangerous. A company that starts raising with six months of runway will be out of money before the process finishes.

The compression point matters most. Investors compare you against their other deals, and a round that is open for a year looks like a round nobody wanted. Running a focused window creates the competition that produces a term sheet.

## Worked example

    Month 1-2   target list, materials, warm intros
    Month 3     30 first meetings in 3 weeks
    Month 4     second meetings, 3-4 serious conversations
    Month 5     term sheets, negotiation
    Month 6     diligence, legal, close

Starting this with four months of runway means the company is out of cash at month 4 — before the term sheet. The fix is not raising faster; it is starting earlier, which is why [runway](#runway) is the number that governs the whole process.

## Watch for

- **A term sheet is not money.** Diligence and legal can take six weeks, and a term sheet can be withdrawn. Do not stop raising until the funds clear.
- **Fundraising consumes the founders.** The people who should be running the business are pitching for a quarter. Plan the operating plan around that.
- **Momentum is real.** A round that closes quickly attracts more interest; one that drags loses it. Compress the window deliberately.
steps: Build a target list of investors who fund your stage and sector.
Warm the introductions before you need them.
Pitch to many investors in a compressed window to create competition.
Run diligence: customers, numbers, references, legal.
Negotiate the term sheet, then close.
inputs: a plan that justifies the amount
entries.cadence: a round typically takes 3-6 months from first pitch to close

entries.title: The Funnel
entries.one_line_definition: The sequence of stages a person moves through from first hearing about you to becoming a customer.
entries.why_it_matters: It turns a vague notion of marketing into measurable stages. Without it you cannot tell whether the problem is awareness, conversion, or retention.
entries.body:
A funnel is a model of how strangers become customers: awareness, interest, consideration, purchase. Each stage loses people, and the point of the model is to see where the losses are.

Without it, marketing decisions are made on totals. "We need more customers" is not actionable. "Our trial-to-paid conversion is 4% against an industry 12%" is.

## Worked example

    Stage                     Count    Conversion
    Ad impressions            100,000      —
    Clicks                      2,000     2.0%
    Signups                       400      20%
    Activated                    160      40%
    Paid                          64      40%

The worst step is impressions to clicks at 2%. But the biggest absolute loss is signups to activated: 400 people sign up and 240 never reach the value. Fixing onboarding from 40% to 60% would take paid customers from 64 to 96 — a 50% increase in revenue from the same traffic.

## Watch for

- **Optimise the worst stage, not the biggest number.** Ten thousand more impressions means nothing if activation is broken.
- **Stages must be defined by behaviour, not by your org chart.** "Marketing-qualified lead" is a handoff, not a customer action.
- **A funnel hides the loop.** Customers who refer others create a second path in. See [channels](#channels) for the economics of each path.
entries.when_to_use: Whenever you need to find where a growth problem actually is, rather than guessing.
entries.when_not_to_use: For products with no repeat purchase, where a loop matters more than a funnel.
steps: Define the stages from first touch to purchase.
Measure how many people enter each stage.
Measure how many convert to the next.
Find the stage with the worst conversion and fix that one first.
entries.limitations: A funnel describes a linear path that real customers do not follow. It is a diagnostic, not a map of behaviour.

entries.title: Gross Margin
entries.one_line_definition: Revenue left over after the cost of producing what you sold.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the pool from which every operating expense is paid. No gross margin means no business, whatever the revenue line says.
entries.body:
Gross margin is the money you keep from each sale after paying to make the thing
you sold. It is the ceiling on everything else: if gross margin is 40%, then
sales, marketing, engineering, and rent all have to fit inside 40% of revenue,
and the remainder is profit or loss.

Two things make it worth learning properly. First, it is the number investors
ask for before they ask for growth — a business with 90% gross margin can lose
money for years and still be a good business; one with 15% cannot. Second, it
is the number pricing decisions show up in first, before volume or CAC.

## Worked example

Same reseller as [cogs](#cogs):

- Revenue: $1,000,000
- COGS: $370,000

    Gross margin = (1,000,000 - 370,000) / 1,000,000 = 63%

If the company spends $400,000 on operating expenses, operating profit is
$230,000, or 23% of revenue. If COGS rises to $500,000 with revenue flat,
gross margin falls to 50% and operating profit falls to $100,000 — a 57% drop
in profit from a 35% rise in COGS. That asymmetry is why this ratio gets so
much attention.

## Watch for

- **Gross margin is not profit.** It ignores every operating expense. Companies
  routinely celebrate 70% gross margin while losing money overall.
- **Contribution margin is the stricter sibling.** Gross margin still carries
  fixed production overhead; contribution margin strips variable selling costs
  too. See [contribution-margin](#contribution-margin).
- **A one-off price cut shows up here, not in volume.** If margin drops while
  revenue rises, you bought revenue.
entries.formula: Gross margin % = (revenue - COGS) / revenue
entries.how_to_read: Compare it to your own history and to the model, never to another industry. A 20% gross margin is fatal in software and normal in grocery.

entries.title: The Hiring Loop
entries.one_line_definition: The repeating cycle of deciding what work needs doing, finding someone who can do it, and verifying they can.
entries.why_it_matters: A bad hire costs more than an empty seat. The loop exists because hiring is a decision under uncertainty, and the cost of getting it wrong compounds through everything that person touches.
entries.body:
Hiring is a loop, not an event, because the alternative is a panic hire when someone leaves. A maintained pipeline turns a crisis into a decision.

The failure mode is hiring for activity instead of outcome. A job description listing tools and years produces candidates who can name the tools. Describing the result the role owns produces candidates who can describe producing it.

## Worked example

Two versions of the same role:

    Bad:   "We need a marketing manager. 3-5 years experience, HubSpot, SEO, paid social."
    Good:  "We need someone who can make our paid channel profitable. You will own CAC from $180 to under $120 in two quarters, and you will tell us what you learned either way."

The second description can be assessed. A candidate who asks "what is the current conversion rate and who is it best for?" is demonstrating the job. One who asks "what is the budget?" is demonstrating that they have not thought about the outcome.

## Watch for

- **Hire slowly, fire quickly.** The asymmetry is brutal: six months of a bad hire costs more than six months of an unfilled role.
- **The interview is a prediction, not a verdict.** Structured questions asked the same way to everyone produce far better predictions than conversation.
- **Reference checks are evidence.** Ask the referee what the person would struggle with, not whether they were good. The answer is almost always honest.
steps: Write the outcome the role must produce, not a list of skills.
Source candidates before you need them.
Assess against the outcome with the same questions every time.
Check the evidence, not the impression.
Make an explicit decision and record the reasoning.
inputs: a clear statement of the outcome the role owns
a structured way to assess them
outputs: or a documented reason the search continues
entries.cadence: continuous; the pipeline should never be empty

entries.title: Incentives Drive Behaviour
entries.one_line_definition: People respond to what they are rewarded and punished for, not to what they are asked to do.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the most reliable predictor of behaviour available. When behaviour contradicts the stated goal, the incentive structure is usually the explanation.
entries.body:
Incentives are the consequences attached to actions, and they predict behaviour better than instructions, culture, or personality. People do what they are paid to do, where "paid" includes money, status, and avoidance of trouble.

The practical use is diagnostic. When behaviour is wrong, look at what the behaviour is rewarded by before concluding that people are careless. The behaviour is usually rational given the incentive.

## Worked example

A support team is measured on tickets closed per day:

    Incentive:      close tickets fast
    Behaviour:      agents close tickets without solving them, then reopen them under a new ticket
    Result:         the metric looks excellent and customer satisfaction falls

The same team measured on resolution at first contact behaves completely differently. Nothing about the people changed. The incentive moved, and the behaviour followed.

## Watch for

- **Incentives are never neutral.** A metric chosen for measurement becomes a target, and people optimise for it. Pick metrics that survive being gamed.
- **Non-financial incentives are incentives.** Recognition, visibility, and who gets promoted all shape behaviour as strongly as pay.
- **Check incentives before blaming people.** The question is "what is this behaviour rewarded by?" — not "why are they like this?"
entries.statement: Show me how someone is rewarded and I will show you how they behave. The stated policy is decoration; the incentive is the mechanism.
entries.evidence: Sales teams paid on volume discount heavily; teams paid on margin do not. The behaviour tracks the reward in every observed case, regardless of the policy manual.
entries.failure_mode: Asking for one behaviour while rewarding another, then treating the resulting behaviour as a character problem rather than a design problem.

entries.title: Inflation
entries.one_line_definition: A general rise in prices, which is the same thing as a fall in what money is worth.
entries.why_it_matters: It quietly changes every number in the business. A price that holds for three years is a price cut, and a cost that rises slower than inflation is a saving.
entries.body:
Inflation is the rate at which money buys less over time. It is usually discussed as a cost of living, but for a business it is a force acting on every price, wage, and contract.

The key insight is that inflation is a comparison, not a level. What matters is whether your prices and your costs move at the same speed. A business whose costs rise faster than its prices is shrinking without noticing.

## Worked example

A company signs a three-year contract at $10,000 a month. Inflation runs at 5% a year:

    Year 1   $10,000 nominal   = $10,000 real
    Year 2   $10,000 nominal   =  $9,524 real
    Year 3   $10,000 nominal   =  $9,070 real

The price never changed, but the customer is paying $930 less in real terms each year by year three — a 9.3% real price cut. Meanwhile the company's own costs, which rise with inflation, are up 10.2%. The margin compresses from both sides.

## Watch for

- **Fixed-price contracts are inflation exposure.** Build in an escalation clause, or the contract becomes a subsidy to the customer.
- **Wages lag inflation, then catch up.** Real wages fall first, which is pleasant for the employer, then resentment builds and the correction is sudden.
- **Inflation changes the hurdle for investment.** A project returning 6% looks good at 2% inflation and worthless at 7%.
entries.formula: Real value = nominal value / (1 + inflation rate)
entries.how_to_read: Read every financial number as nominal or real. A contract with a fixed price for five years is exposed to inflation the customer will eventually notice.

entries.title: Interest Rates
entries.one_line_definition: The price of borrowing money, which is also the discount the market applies to future cash.
entries.why_it_matters: It sets the cost of capital and the value of waiting. A change in rates changes which projects are worth doing and how much a growing company is worth.
entries.body:
An interest rate is the price of money over time. It matters to a business in two ways: directly, as the cost of any borrowing, and indirectly, as the rate at which future cash is discounted to a present value.

The second effect is the one founders miss. A dollar of profit in five years is worth less than a dollar today, and the higher the rate, the less it is worth. Rising rates therefore punish long-horizon, capital-heavy businesses and favour ones that return cash quickly.

## Worked example

A project returns $1,000,000 in five years. Its present value at different rates:

    At 3%:   1,000,000 / 1.03^5 = $862,609
    At 7%:   1,000,000 / 1.07^5 = $712,986
    At 12%:  1,000,000 / 1.12^5 = $567,427

The same future cash is worth $295,182 less at 12% than at 3%. A company planning on a distant payoff is worth a third less purely because rates moved — with no change to the business.

## Watch for

- **Rates set the value of growth.** High rates make "grow now, profit later" expensive. That is why growth companies are hit hardest when rates rise.
- **Your runway is a rate-sensitive asset.** See [runway](#runway). Borrowing to extend it costs more when rates are high.
- **Cheap money creates bad habits.** Projects funded at 1% that would fail at 6% get built, and the failures surface only when rates normalise.
entries.formula: Present value = future cash / (1 + rate)^years
entries.how_to_read: Read it as the opportunity cost of capital. If you can earn 5% risk-free, a business project must beat that or it destroys value.

entries.title: Intellectual Property
entries.one_line_definition: The legal rights over creations of the mind — inventions, designs, names, and written work.
entries.why_it_matters: It is often the only asset a young company has that cannot be copied overnight, and it is frequently lost by inattention rather than by theft.
entries.body:
Intellectual property is the law's way of protecting things you can copy but cannot touch. The main types are patents for inventions, trademarks for names and marks, copyright for written and creative work, and trade secrets for information kept confidential.
