The practical point for a young company is that IP is often lost through process, not through a competitor. An employee who invents something may own it, not the company, unless the contract says otherwise.

## Worked example

A software company with a distinctive name and a novel algorithm:

    Copyright      The source code is protected automatically on creation. Registration helps enforce it.
    Trademark      The name must be registered to be defended reliably; an unregistered mark is hard to stop others using.
    Patent         The algorithm may be patentable, but software patents are slow, expensive, and jurisdiction-dependent.
    Trade secret   The customer list and pricing are protected only if access is controlled and contracts say so.

The most common failure: a contractor builds the product, and nothing in their contract assigns the IP to the company. The company then owns nothing it paid for, and the contractor can sell the same code to a competitor.

## Watch for

- **IP must be assigned in writing.** A contractor, co-founder, or early employee who creates something owns it by default in many jurisdictions unless a contract says otherwise.
- **Registration is not optional for trademarks.** A name you use is not a name you own.
- **IP is a moat, not a product.** Owning a patent does not make customers want the product. See [moat](#moat).
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a set of separate rights with different rules. A patent, a trademark, and copyright protect different things and last different lengths.

entries.title: Jobs to be Done
entries.one_line_definition: The progress a customer is trying to make in a particular circumstance, which is what they actually hire a product to do.
entries.why_it_matters: It redefines the competitor set. You do not compete with similar products; you compete with everything the customer could do instead, including doing nothing.
entries.body:
Jobs to be Done says customers do not buy products; they hire them to make progress. The classic example is a drill: nobody wants a drill, they want a hole, and the hole is a means to hanging a shelf.

The practical payoff is a competitor set that includes everything else the customer might do. The rival to a project-management tool is not another tool — it is the spreadsheet, the email thread, and the decision to do nothing.

## Worked example

A customer buys a bookkeeping app. The surface answer is "they want accounting software." The job is different:

    Functional:  know whether the business made money this month
    Emotional:   stop feeling anxious about the numbers
    Social:      look credible to an accountant or investor
    Circumstance: it is the first month they have been too busy to keep up

The competitor set is now spreadsheets, an accountant, a bookkeeping service, and ignoring it. Each competes on different terms. An app that wins on "stop feeling anxious" — by showing a single plain-English number on day one — beats one with more features but a steeper learning curve.

## Watch for

- **The job is not the feature.** "They asked for a dashboard" is a solution, not a job. Ask what progress they wanted from the dashboard.
- **Circumstance is the unit.** The same person has different jobs in different situations. Segment by circumstance, not by demographic.
- **Doing nothing is a competitor.** Most products lose to inaction, not to a rival. If the customer's current state is tolerable, you have no job to win.
entries.when_to_use: When positioning, when a feature request does not make sense, or when you need to understand why customers really buy.
entries.when_not_to_use: As a substitute for talking to customers. The framework structures interviews; it does not replace them.
steps: Identify the functional job the customer is trying to accomplish.
Identify the emotional and social dimensions of that job.
Identify the circumstances that make the job urgent.
List every alternative the customer considers, including doing nothing.
Design against the job, not against the feature request.
entries.limitations: Jobs are hard to identify and easy to invent. A job you have imagined will produce a product nobody hires.

entries.title: Lifetime Value
entries.one_line_definition: The total profit a customer generates over the whole relationship.
entries.why_it_matters: It sets the ceiling on what you can afford to spend acquiring that customer. Without it, CAC is just a number.
entries.body:
Lifetime value is the profit a customer produces from the day they arrive to the day they leave. It is the other half of the unit-economics equation: CAC tells you what a customer costs, LTV tells you what they are worth.

The two together decide whether growth is worth buying. A customer worth more than they cost to acquire makes growth cheap. A customer who costs more than they return makes growth a way to lose money faster.

## Worked example

A subscription costs $30 a month with a contribution margin of $21 after variable costs. The average customer stays 14 months:

    LTV = 21 x 14 = 294

If acquiring that customer costs $98, the ratio is 294 / 98 = 3.0x, and the customer pays back in about 4.7 months. Now suppose churn rises so the average stay falls to 7 months:

    LTV = 21 x 7 = 147
    LTV/CAC = 147 / 98 = 1.5x

The acquisition cost did not change. The business halved its value per customer, which is why churn and LTV are the same conversation.

## Watch for

- **Use contribution margin, not revenue.** Gross margin is a reasonable proxy; revenue is not, because it ignores the cost of serving the customer.
- **LTV is an average.** Averages hide the difference between customers who stay two months and customers who stay two years.
- **Cohort, not aggregate.** An LTV computed across all customers mixes old cohorts with new ones and hides whether newer customers are better or worse.
entries.formula: LTV = contribution margin per period x number of periods retained
entries.how_to_read: Read it against CAC, never alone. A large LTV is meaningless if the customer costs more than that to acquire.

entries.title: Mental Models
entries.one_line_definition: A compact representation of how something works, used to reason about a situation without re-deriving it from scratch.
entries.why_it_matters: They multiply the decisions you can make well. A good model turns a novel situation into a recognised one, which is the difference between a considered choice and a guess.
entries.body:
A mental model is a simplified picture of how a domain works — supply and demand, incentives, [opportunity cost](#opportunity-cost), [second-order thinking](#second-order-thinking). They are useful because the world is too complex to reason about directly, and a model compresses it.

The danger is forgetting that the map is not the territory. A model that explains most situations will mislead in the one that matters, and the confidence it produces is the warning sign.

## Worked example

Deciding whether to raise prices:

    Model: demand curve        — higher price, lower volume. Ask: how elastic is this market?
    Model: anchoring           — the new price becomes the reference for all future comparisons.
    Model: incentives          — what does the change reward the sales team to do?
    Model: second-order        — existing customers see the increase; what does that do to trust?

No single model answers the question. Four models together surface the trade-offs that one alone would hide. That is the actual value of a model collection: not answers, but a checklist of angles.

## Watch for

- **A model is a prompt, not a conclusion.** The right output of a model is a question, not an answer.
- **Using one model is worse than using none.** A single lens feels like clarity and is usually just a blind spot.
- **Models expire.** A model that explained a market at one scale may not explain it at another.
entries.how_to_read: Read them as tools, not truths. A model is a simplification, and its value is in the questions it prompts — not in being right.

entries.title: Moat
entries.one_line_definition: A structural advantage that makes it hard for competitors to take your customers.
entries.why_it_matters: Without one, competition drives your price toward cost and your margin toward zero. The moat is what keeps the profit you create.
entries.body:
A moat is a durable reason a customer stays with you even when a competitor offers the same thing cheaper. It is the economic term for defensibility.

The test is not whether you are better today. It is whether a well-funded competitor could replicate your offer in a year and take your customers. If they can, you have a lead, not a moat — and leads expire.

## Worked example

Four businesses, same product category, four different positions:

    A. Better UI            — copied in a quarter. No moat.
    B. Lower price          — undercut tomorrow. No moat.
    C. Data from 40,000 users that improves the product — copying the feature does not copy the data. Moat.
    D. Contracts running to 2028 with switching costs — a competitor must wait or pay to displace them. Moat.

A and B compete on effort, which anyone can match. C and D compete on accumulated position, which takes years to build and cannot be bought quickly.

## Watch for

- **A moat is not a feature.** Features are copied. Moats are network effects, switching costs, economies of scale, and regulation.
- **Moats can be temporary.** Technology changes destroy them. A retailer's location moat died with the internet.
- **Moats protect margin, not existence.** They let you keep profit; they do not make you immune to a market that stops wanting the product.
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a question: what happens to a competitor who copies your product exactly? If the answer is 'nothing much', you have no moat.

entries.title: Minimum Viable Product
entries.one_line_definition: The smallest thing you can build that tests whether a customer will pay for the value you believe exists.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the cheapest way to find out whether you are wrong. Every month spent building before that test is a month of unverified assumption.
entries.body:
An MVP is not a smaller version of the final product. It is an experiment: the minimum build that can test the riskiest assumption behind the business.

The distinction matters because most "MVPs" are actually incomplete products. A product missing its core value cannot test demand — it can only test whether people tolerate missing features.

## Worked example

A company believes small firms will pay $50 a month for automated invoicing. Two approaches:

    Approach A — build the full product: recurring billing, integrations, reporting, mobile app. Six months. Then launch and find out.
    Approach B — build only invoice generation, deliver it manually behind the scenes, charge from day one. Two weeks.

Approach B tests the real assumption: will someone pay? If 10 customers pay, the company knows to build Approach A. If none do, it spent two weeks instead of six months. The manual work is not a shortcut — it is the point, because it buys certainty.

## Watch for

- **The assumption must be named.** "Test whether people want this" is untestable. "Test whether a 20-person firm pays $50 for automated reminders" is.
- **An MVP can be a conversation.** A landing page, a priced offer, or a manual service can all be MVPs. Shipping code is the most expensive option.
- **MVPs accumulate debt.** The shortcut is only valid if you plan to rebuild. Otherwise the experiment becomes the product.
entries.how_to_read: Read 'viable' as 'capable of producing a real answer', not 'small and broken'. An MVP that cannot deliver the core value tests nothing.

entries.title: Network Effects
entries.one_line_definition: When each additional customer makes the product more valuable for every existing customer.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the strongest moat there is, because the advantage grows automatically with use and a competitor must overcome the network, not just the product.
entries.body:
A network effect means the product's value is a function of how many people use it. Telephones, marketplaces, and payment networks all become more useful as they grow.

The consequence is a winner-take-most dynamic. Once a network passes a tipping point, customers are not choosing the better product — they are choosing the one their contacts already use, and no amount of feature work overcomes that.

## Worked example

A messaging app's value to a user is roughly the share of their contacts on it:

    20% of contacts on it   →  you check two apps. Slightly useful.
    60% of contacts on it   →  you move most conversations. Clearly useful.
    90% of contacts on it   →  leaving means losing touch with everyone.

The jump from 60% to 90% is where the moat forms. A competitor with better features at 5% share offers less value than the incumbent at 90%, because value came from the network, not the features. That is why network-effect markets usually produce one dominant player.

## Watch for

- **Not every user adds value.** A social network full of accounts that never post does not strengthen the network. Density within a community matters more than total users.
- **Network effects can be local.** A marketplace can be strong in one city and weak in another; growth must be concentrated, not spread.
- **They decay.** If the network stops being useful — spam, noise, irrelevance — the same mechanism accelerates the exit.
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a growth curve with a tipping point. Below the point the product is worse than the alternative; above it, leaving costs more than staying.

entries.title: Operating Expenses
entries.one_line_definition: The cost of running the business that is not tied to producing a specific unit sold.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the part of the cost base you control. COGS scales with sales; operating expenses scale with decisions.
entries.body:
Operating expenses — opex — are the costs of keeping the lights on: salaries for people who do not build the product, rent, software, marketing, legal, and the sales team's overhead. They are the costs that remain even if you sell nothing.

The distinction from COGS is the distinction between *variable* and *fixed* cost. COGS goes up when you sell more; opex mostly does not. That is why opex is where leverage lives: a company whose opex is flat while revenue doubles sees its margin expand without changing the product at all.

## Worked example

A SaaS company:

- Revenue: $1,000,000
- COGS (hosting, support): $150,000
- Operating expenses: $700,000 — engineering $350,000, sales and marketing $250,000, general and administrative $100,000

    Gross margin = 1,000,000 - 150,000 = 850,000  (85%)
    Operating profit = 850,000 - 700,000 = 150,000  (15%)

Now revenue doubles to $2,000,000 with COGS rising to $300,000 and opex rising only to $850,000:

    Gross margin = 2,000,000 - 300,000 = 1,700,000  (85%)
    Operating profit = 1,700,000 - 850,000 = 850,000  (42.5%)

Revenue doubled, profit grew 5.7x. That asymmetry is operating leverage, and it is the reason investors care about the opex line.

## Watch for

- **Opex is a choice, not a fact.** Hiring, office space, and tooling are decisions. Treating them as fixed is how costs creep.
- **See [break-even](#break-even)** — opex is the fixed cost you must cover before any sale becomes profit.
- **Capitalised costs hide here.** Software development is often capitalised rather than expensed, which flatters this line and moves the cost to the balance sheet.
entries.formula: Operating profit = gross margin - operating expenses
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a ratio to revenue, over time. A rising ratio with flat revenue means the business is getting more expensive to run.

entries.title: Opportunity Cost
entries.one_line_definition: What you give up by choosing one option over the next best alternative.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the difference between a decision and a wish. Every choice spends money, time, and attention that cannot be spent again.
entries.body:
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you did not choose. It is not a line on a balance sheet — it never appears in the accounts — which is exactly why it is so often ignored.

A decision is only rational when the chosen option beats the alternative, not when it beats nothing. Building a feature for three months is profitable if the alternative was nothing; it is a loss if the alternative was a feature that would have brought in twice the revenue.

## Worked example

You have one engineer for a quarter. Two options:

- **Option A** — rebuild the checkout: costs $60,000 in salary, expected to lift conversion by 2%, worth $200,000 a year.
- **Option B** — fix the onboarding funnel: costs $60,000, expected to lift activation by 10%, worth $120,000 a year.

Option A looks better on its own. But choosing A means the $120,000 from B is the opportunity cost. The comparison is:

    A net:  200,000 - 120,000 = 80,000
    B net:  120,000 - 200,000 = -80,000

A still wins, but by half what it looked like. If B had been worth $250,000, A would have been the wrong call despite the bigger headline number.

## Watch for

- **Sunk costs are not opportunity costs.** Money already spent is gone and should not weigh on the decision. Only the forward-looking alternatives matter.
- **Time is the hidden one.** Two options costing the same cash can have very different opportunity costs if one takes three times as long.
- **See [pricing](#pricing)** — the same discipline applies to price: a discount's real cost is the full-price sale you gave up.
entries.how_to_read: If two options look equal on paper, the one with the lower opportunity cost wins. If the cost is invisible, it is probably being ignored.

entries.title: CAC Payback Period
entries.one_line_definition: How many months of a customer's contribution it takes to recover the cost of acquiring them.
entries.why_it_matters: It converts CAC from a cost into a cash-flow event. A CAC that pays back in two months is cheap; the same CAC at two years is a loan you may not survive.
entries.body:
Payback period is the time a customer takes to pay for their own acquisition. It is the bridge between unit economics and cash flow, and it is the number investors check most often after CAC and LTV.

The distinction it makes is between a cost that returns quickly and a cost that ties up capital. Two businesses can have identical CAC and LTV and completely different cash situations purely because of payback.

## Worked example

CAC is $300. The customer pays $50 a month with a contribution margin of $35:

    Payback = 300 / 35 = 8.6 months

Now the same customer on a $20 plan with a $14 contribution margin:

    Payback = 300 / 14 = 21.4 months

Same acquisition cost. The cheaper plan takes 21 months to pay for itself, which means the business must finance the customer for over a year and a half. That is why a low-price plan with the same CAC can be far worse than a high-price one.

## Watch for

- **Use contribution margin, not revenue.** Paying back on revenue flatters the number; the cost of serving the customer is real.
- **Payback sets your capital need.** Adding customers adds to the amount you must finance. Growth beyond your capital is a funding problem, not a sales problem.
- **Longer payback needs longer customers.** If payback is 12 months and the average customer stays 10, the customer never pays for itself. See [ltv](#ltv).
entries.formula: Payback = CAC / monthly contribution margin per customer
entries.how_to_read: Under twelve months is healthy for most subscription businesses. Over twelve months you are funding your customers and need capital to do it.

entries.title: Pipeline
entries.one_line_definition: The total value of opportunities in play, weighted by how likely each is to close.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the forward view of the business. Revenue is a lagging indicator; pipeline is the leading one, and it is the only thing you can act on early.
entries.body:
Pipeline is the set of deals that might close, each valued and weighted by probability. It is how a sales organisation sees the future, and it is the earliest warning available.

The distinction from a forecast matters. A forecast is a promise; a pipeline is a picture. A pipeline tells you where the risk is — too few opportunities, or too many stuck at low probability — while there is still time to do something about it.

## Worked example

    Opportunity        Value    Probability   Weighted
    Acme               40,000       60%        24,000
    Beta                25,000       40%        10,000
    Gamma               60,000       80%        48,000
    Delta               15,000       10%         1,500
    Total              140,000                  83,500

Quota is $200,000 for the quarter. Weighted pipeline coverage is 83,500 / 200,000 = 0.4x, far below the 3x usually needed. The problem is visible: Delta is nearly dead weight and Beta is unlikely. Those two need attention now, not at quarter end.

## Watch for

- **Probabilities are opinions.** Salespeople optimise them. Require evidence for a high probability and audit the ones that never move.
- **Coverage is a ratio, not a total.** A large pipeline against a large quota can be as unhealthy as a small one against a small quota.
- **Stale pipeline is worse than no pipeline.** An opportunity that has not moved in two months should be removed. It inflates coverage while hiding the gap.
entries.formula: Weighted pipeline = sum of (deal value x probability of closing)
entries.how_to_read: Read it as coverage against quota, not as a forecast. A pipeline three times quota is healthy; one that merely equals quota is a coin flip.

entries.title: Positioning
entries.one_line_definition: The specific place you want to own in the customer's mind, relative to alternatives.
entries.why_it_matters: It decides what you are compared against. Competing on someone else's terms means their criteria win, and you lose.
entries.body:
Positioning is the deliberate choice of what you are and are not. It is not a slogan; it is a decision about which comparison you want to be judged in.

A clear position makes every other decision easier. Pricing, features, channels, and messaging all follow from it. A vague position makes every decision arbitrary, which is why undifferentiated products compete on price and always lose.

## Worked example

A project-management tool could position against "spreadsheets" or against "Jira."

- Against spreadsheets: for teams that outgrew them. Message: "your spreadsheet breaks at fifty rows." Buyer: a small team, price-sensitive, short sales cycle.
- Against Jira: for teams that find Jira too heavy. Message: "real work, not ticket queues." Buyer: an engineering team, higher budget, longer cycle.

Both describe the same software. They are different products to different buyers, at different prices, through different channels. Picking one is positioning; picking neither is competing on price against both.

## Watch for

- **Positioning is a sacrifice.** Saying you are for everyone means you are for no one. The excluded segment is the point.
- **It must be defensible.** A position the market does not believe is just marketing. See [competitive-advantage](#competitive-advantage).
- **Positioning precedes messaging.** Writing copy before deciding the position produces words that describe features instead of a reason to buy.
entries.how_to_read: If a sentence cannot say who you are for and why you are different, you do not have a position — you have a description.

entries.title: Pricing
entries.one_line_definition: What you charge, and the logic that decides it.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the fastest lever on profit. A price change flows straight to the bottom line with no change in cost, volume, or product.
entries.body:
Pricing is the most under-used lever in business. Founders price from cost or from competitors; the better question is what the customer's alternative costs them.

Cost-plus pricing ignores the customer entirely. Competitor-based pricing hands over the decision about your value to someone else. Value-based pricing asks what the customer would otherwise pay — in money, time, or risk — and captures a share of that.

## Worked example

A tool saves a bookkeeper 10 hours a month. A bookkeeper costs $40 an hour, so the value is $400 a month:

    Value-based price:  $40–80/month  (captures 10–20% of value)
    Cost-plus price:    $15/month     (cost + margin)
    Competitor price:   $50/month     (whatever the rival charges)

The cost-plus price leaves $385 of value with the customer. That is not generosity; it is money left on the table that funds your competitor's growth. A price of $60 captures a fair share and still saves the customer $340.

## Watch for

- **Price is a signal.** A price far below the value signals low quality; a price far above it invites a competitor. The wrong signal costs more than the wrong number.
- **Anchoring matters.** The first number the customer sees shapes every later comparison. Discounting trains them to wait for discounts.
- **Raise prices on the existing base last.** Existing customers are the hardest to re-price and the most visible. Test on new customers first.
entries.formula: Price = value to the customer, captured at a sustainable share
entries.how_to_read: Read price against contribution margin and against the customer's alternative. If the customer cannot see the value, the price is too high regardless of your costs.

entries.title: Pricing Change
entries.one_line_definition: A checklist for changing your price without breaking your business.
entries.why_it_matters: Pricing is the highest-leverage decision a business makes, and the one most often made on vibes.
entries.body:
A price change is not a number change. It is a claim about who your product is
for and what it is worth. Most teams treat it as a spreadsheet exercise and are
surprised when the spreadsheet is right and the business breaks anyway.

## Before you change anything

Answer the four questions in the trigger. If you cannot answer "what is the
value to the customer" in one sentence, stop. You are not ready to price; you
are ready to learn.

## The test

Test the new price on new customers first. Existing customers carry switching
costs and goodwill that distort the signal. A price that works on new customers
and fails on old ones is a communication problem, not a pricing problem.

## The rollout

Grandfather existing customers for a fixed period, then migrate. Announce the
change before it takes effect, with the reason. Customers tolerate a price
increase they understand and resent one they discover on their invoice.

## The number that matters

Gross margin at the new price, at the same volume. If volume drops, the question
is whether the margin gain exceeds the revenue loss. That is arithmetic, and
it is the only part of this that is.
entries.trigger: You are considering changing your price, and need to know whether to do it, by how much, and how to roll it out.
questions: What is the value to the customer, not the cost to you?
Who is the marginal customer you would lose?
What does the current price signal about who you are?
Can you test before committing?
numbers_to_pull: Gross margin at current price
Price elasticity from past changes or competitor data
Churn rate by price tier
Customer acquisition cost at current price
traps: Pricing to cost instead of to value
Raising price without changing the offer
Testing on existing customers before new ones
Ignoring the signal price sends to the market

entries.title: Product-market Fit
entries.one_line_definition: The degree to which the product satisfies a real demand from a defined group of customers.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the precondition for everything else. Growth before fit accelerates a product nobody wants; fit without growth is a hobby.
entries.body:
Product-market fit is the point where a real group of customers wants what you have enough to keep paying for it. It is not the same as having users, or having revenue, or having a good product.

The distinction matters because the failure modes are different. Before fit, growth spending is wasted — you are filling a bucket with no bottom. After fit, growth spending compounds, because the customers who arrive stay.

## Worked example

The standard test asks users how they would feel without the product. In a survey of 200:

    Very disappointed   90   (45%)
    Somewhat disappointed 60   (30%)
    Not disappointed     50   (25%)

Above 40% "very disappointed" is the usual threshold for fit. Now suppose the same survey a quarter earlier:

    Very disappointed   55   (27%)

The product was close but not there. Spending on paid acquisition at 27% would have bought customers who left; at 45% the same spend compounds.

## Watch for

- **Fit is per segment.** A product can have fit with one group and none with another. Segment before concluding.
- **Fit decays.** A market changes and competitors appear. The survey is a snapshot, not a permanent state.
- **Fit is not traction.** A waiting list is interest, not fit. Fit requires that customers stay and pay once the novelty fades.
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a threshold, not a feeling. If customers would be very disappointed without the product, you have it. If they would shrug, you do not.

entries.title: Quota and Coverage
entries.one_line_definition: The revenue target assigned to a seller, and the pipeline multiple required to make it achievable.
entries.why_it_matters: Quota is the mechanism that connects company revenue to individual behaviour. Set it wrong and you either pay for failure or leave money uncollected.
entries.body:
Quota is the individual revenue target that, summed across the team, makes the company plan. Coverage is how much pipeline must exist to make that quota realistic rather than hopeful.

The two are a system. Quota without coverage is a wish; coverage without quota is activity with no target. Setting them together is the core of sales management.

## Worked example

A seller closes 20% of qualified opportunities and has a 60-day cycle. Quota is $120,000 for the quarter:

    Needed closed value      = 120,000
    Needed opportunities     = 120,000 / 20% = 600,000 in pipeline
    Coverage                  = 600,000 / 120,000 = 5.0x

At a 20% win rate the seller needs five times quota in pipeline. Now raise the win rate to 40% with better qualification:

    Needed opportunities     = 120,000 / 40% = 300,000
    Coverage                  = 2.5x

The same quota became half as demanding — not by working harder, but by qualifying better. That is why coverage ratios should be derived from actual win rates, not copied from a benchmark.

## Watch for

- **Attainment should cluster near 60-70%.** Everyone hitting quota means it is too low; almost nobody hitting it means it is demotivating and wrong.
- **Quota is a commitment, not a ceiling.** Capping earnings turns high performers into the people who stop trying.
- **Coverage differs by segment.** A new-logo motion needs more coverage than an expansion motion. Blending them produces a number that fits neither.
entries.formula: Pipeline coverage needed = historical win rate and cycle length, typically 3-4x quota
entries.how_to_read: Read quota against attainment history. If half the team misses every quarter, the quota is wrong, not the team.

entries.title: Raising a Round
entries.one_line_definition: A checklist for deciding whether to raise, and what to expect when you do.
entries.why_it_matters: Fundraising is a full-time job disguised as a side project, and most founders start it without knowing the rules.
entries.body:
Raising money is not a milestone. It is a trade: you give up a permanent share
of a business that may be worth something later, in exchange for time and
resources now. The trade is worth making only when the time and resources buy
something revenue cannot.

## Before you start

Answer the four questions. If the answer to "what will you do with it that you
cannot do with revenue" is "grow faster," you have not answered the question.
Faster is not a use of funds; it is an outcome. The use of funds is specific:
hire three engineers, open a second market, fund a twelve-month sales cycle.

## The process

Fundraising is a sales process with a single buyer at a time. Treat it like
one. Run a tight timeline, create competition between investors, and never let
one investor's pace set your company's pace.

## The terms

Valuation is the number people remember. The terms are the numbers that matter.
Liquidation preference, participation, anti-dilution, and board composition
decide who gets paid and who decides. Read the term sheet twice, and have a
lawyer read it once more.

## The cost

The real cost of a round is not the dilution. It is the reporting, the board
meetings, the investor updates, and the loss of the ability to change your mind
quietly. Count that cost before you take the money.
entries.trigger: You are considering raising external capital, and need to know whether you should, on what terms, and from whom.
questions: Do you need the money, or do you want the signal?
What will you do with it that you cannot do with revenue?
What does your cap table look like after this round?
Who on your team will run the process while you keep running the company?
numbers_to_pull: Monthly burn and runway
Revenue growth rate, trailing 12 months
CAC and LTV by channel
Current cap table and dilution model
traps: Raising before you have a story the numbers support
Optimizing for valuation over investor fit
Letting the process stall the product
Ignoring the liquidation preference

entries.title: Retention and Cohorts
entries.one_line_definition: The share of customers who are still using the product after a given period.
entries.why_it_matters: Retention is the compounding engine. It determines whether growth accumulates or leaks, and it is the input to every lifetime-value calculation.
entries.body:
Retention is the complement of churn: the customers who stay. But it is more useful than churn as a lens, because it can be read over time and because its shape is diagnostic.

A retention curve that drops steeply and then flattens is healthy — it means the customers who remain are the ones who genuinely need the product. A curve that declines linearly is unhealthy — it means the product never becomes part of the customer's routine.

## Worked example

    Cohort of 1,000 customers acquired in January
      Month 1:  800 active  (80%)
      Month 3:  560 active  (56%)
      Month 6:  430 active  (43%)
      Month 12: 390 active  (39%)

The curve flattens after month 6. The 390 who remain are the durable base, and the business can plan around them. Compare a second cohort that declines linearly to 15% by month 12: the product is attracting a different kind of customer, or the onboarding is worse.

## Watch for

- **Aggregate retention hides everything.** It mixes new and old cohorts and rises as the base grows even when each cohort is getting worse.
- **Cohort by acquisition date, not by activity.** Group customers by when they arrived; that is the only grouping that reveals a trend.
- **Retention is not engagement.** A customer who logs in daily and still cancels is a churn risk. Retention measures whether they stay, not whether they are happy.
entries.formula: Retention = customers still active / customers at start
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a curve over time, not a single number. The shape of the curve tells you more than its level.

entries.title: Revenue
entries.one_line_definition: The total money a business brings in from selling its product or service.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the top line every other number is measured against, and the number most often confused with success.
entries.body:
Revenue is the gross inflow from sales before any costs are deducted. It is the first line of the income statement and the denominator of almost every ratio in this atlas.

Three things make it treacherous. It is not profit — a company can grow revenue while losing money on every sale. It is not cash — revenue is recognised when earned, which may be weeks before the money arrives. And it can be bought — spending on discounts or acquisition can raise revenue while destroying margin.

## Worked example

A company sells 1,000 units a month at $50 each:

    Revenue = 50 x 1,000 = 50,000

Against that: COGS of $20,000 and operating expenses of $25,000.

    Gross margin = 50,000 - 20,000 = 30,000  (60%)
    Operating profit = 30,000 - 25,000 = 5,000  (10%)

Revenue doubled would be $100,000 on paper — but if the extra 1,000 units were sold at a $10 discount and cost $30 each to fulfil, the new units bring in $40,000 of revenue and $10,000 of gross margin. Revenue looks like growth; margin per unit fell from 60% to 25%.

## Watch for

- **Recognised revenue is not cash.** A $120,000 annual contract booked in January may pay monthly. Revenue and cash flow are separate statements.
- **Gross vs net.** Marketplaces and agencies report very different revenue for the same transaction depending on whether they report the full amount or only their fee.
- **See [runway](#runway)** — revenue is the input to whether you survive long enough to be right.
entries.formula: Revenue = price x quantity sold
entries.how_to_read: Revenue is not income and not cash. Read it against cost of goods sold, then against operating expenses, then against the timing of the cash.

entries.title: Reversible vs Irreversible Decisions
entries.one_line_definition: Classifying decisions by whether you can undo them, and matching your process to the class.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the difference between a decision made in a day and one made in a quarter. Treating a reversible decision as irreversible is the most expensive form of caution.
entries.body:
Decisions come in two kinds. A reversible decision can be undone at a cost smaller than the cost of deciding slowly. An irreversible one cannot, or only at a cost that changes the business.

The value of the distinction is speed. Most decisions in a young company are reversible, and treating them as permanent creates a culture where nothing happens without a meeting.

## Worked example

    Decision                          Class          Right process
    Change the pricing page copy      Reversible     Ship it today, measure for a week
    Hire a second engineer            Mostly         Decide in days; you can manage them out
    Sign a 3-year office lease        Irreversible   Diligence, alternatives, board sign-off
    Sunset a feature                  Reversible     Do it; re-add it if customers revolt
    Take venture money                Irreversible   Term sheet, references, long deliberation

The pricing change and the feature sunset are the same kind of decision. One is made in a day and the other in a quarter purely because of habit, and the difference is weeks of learning.

## Watch for

- **Reversibility is about cost, not about regret.** A bad hire can be undone; it is expensive, not irreversible.
- **Speed has a cost too.** A reversible decision made without anyone checking it can still be wrong — the answer is to measure, not to deliberate.
- **Irreversible decisions deserve dissent.** The goal is not consensus but the strongest argument against, stated before the decision is locked.
entries.statement: A reversible decision should be made quickly by the person closest to the information. An irreversible one should be made slowly, with dissent sought out deliberately.
entries.evidence: Organisations that default to consensus for every decision are slow on the decisions that do not matter and rushed on the ones that do, because the process is the same for both.
entries.failure_mode: Applying the same deliberation to everything, so that cheap, undoable experiments are delayed while expensive, permanent commitments are made without scrutiny.

entries.title: Roadmapping
entries.one_line_definition: Deciding the order in which you will build, and communicating that order so the rest of the company can plan around it.
entries.why_it_matters: It converts a backlog into a commitment. Without it, every stakeholder prioritises their own request and nothing ships in a coherent order.
entries.body:
Roadmapping is the discipline of choosing an order and defending it. Its value is not the document — it is the decision about what you will not do, and the communication of that decision.

A roadmap fails in one of two ways: it lists features with no outcome, so it cannot be argued with; or it is treated as a promise, so learning cannot change it.

## Worked example

A team has six candidate items and capacity for three:

    1. Automated reminders      — directly addresses churn in the largest cohort
    2. Reporting dashboard      — requested by sales, no evidence it changes retention
    3. Mobile app               — strategic, but no evidence mobile users retain better
    4. Export to accountant      — cited in 3 of the last 5 churn interviews
    5. New onboarding flow      — activation is 40% against a 60% target
    6. Dark mode                — requested often, unrelated to any outcome

Ranked by evidence against the stated outcome (retention and activation): 5, 1, 4. Item 3 waits for evidence. Item 2 and 6 are explicitly deferred with the reason stated, which is what makes the roadmap credible.

## Watch for

- **Outcomes before outputs.** "Increase activation to 60%" can be argued with. "Ship onboarding flow" cannot.
- **A roadmap is a hypothesis.** If evidence changes, the order should change. A roadmap nobody is allowed to revise becomes a fiction.
- **Silence is not agreement.** Publishing a roadmap and hearing nothing usually means people did not believe it, not that they accepted it.
steps: State the outcome you are aiming for, not the features.
List candidate bets against that outcome.
Rank by evidence and by dependency, not by loudness.
Commit to an order and publish it with the reasoning.
Revisit monthly against what you learned.
outputs: a sequenced set of bets with rationale

entries.title: Return on Ad Spend
entries.one_line_definition: Revenue earned for every dollar spent on advertising.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the fastest honest read on whether a paid channel is pulling its weight, and the number people lie with most.
entries.body:
Return on ad spend is revenue divided by ad spend. It looks like the answer to
"is this channel working", and because it is a single number, it is frequently
the wrong answer.

The reason: ROAS has no costs in it. It tells you how much revenue a dollar of
ads produced, not how much money the business kept. A channel can return 4x and
lose money if the product's contribution margin is 20%, because $4 of revenue
carries only $0.80 of contribution and you spent $1.00 to get it.

The correct pairing is ROAS against contribution margin. Work out the break-even
ROAS for your margin, then judge the channel against that.

## Worked example

A product sells for $100 with a contribution margin of $45 after all variable
costs including processing and fulfilment.

    Break-even ROAS = 1 / 0.45 = 2.22x

Anything above 2.22x makes money on the first purchase; anything below loses
money. Now the channels:

    Paid search:   $3,000 spend → $12,000 revenue  = 4.0x   (profitable)
    Paid social:   $3,000 spend → $ 8,400 revenue  = 2.8x   (profitable, thin)
    Display:       $3,000 spend → $ 6,000 revenue  = 2.0x   (losing money)

Display looks like it "returns 2x", which sounds fine until you see it is below
the 2.22x break-even. It is losing $0.20 on every dollar spent.

## Watch for

- **Attribution is the whole game.** A 4x ROAS from last-click is not the same
  as 4x from a geo holdout. State the model or do not quote the number.
- **Revenue is not profit.** See the break-even calculation above; without it,
  ROAS is a vanity metric.
- **First-purchase ROAS ignores repeat buying.** A customer who buys once at a
  loss and returns three times is good business. Compute ROAS on the cohort's
  lifetime value, not the single order.
entries.formula: ROAS = revenue attributed to ads / ad spend
entries.how_to_read: Read it against contribution margin, never against itself. A 4x ROAS can still be a money loser.

entries.title: Runway
entries.one_line_definition: How many months a company can keep operating before it runs out of cash.
entries.why_it_matters: It sets the deadline on every plan. A strategy that pays off in eighteen months is a bad strategy with six months of runway.
entries.body:
Runway is cash divided by burn. It converts a spending rate into a deadline, and it is the single number that should be on the founder's dashboard.

It is also the number most often misstated. Founders quote runway on gross burn while ignoring revenue, or on a burn rate that has already changed, or on cash that is committed to something else.

## Worked example

- Cash on hand: $900,000
- Monthly burn (net): $150,000

    Runway = 900,000 / 150,000 = 6 months

A fundraise typically takes four to six months from first meeting to cash in the bank. With six months of runway, a founder who starts raising now is raising at the last possible moment, with no leverage and no alternatives. The correct move is to start at twelve months, when there is still a choice.

Now suppose revenue grows so net burn falls to $90,000:

    Runway = 900,000 / 90,000 = 10 months

The cash did not change. The deadline moved four months — which is the whole point of improving unit economics before raising.

## Watch for

- **Runway is not a plan.** It is a constraint. A plan that assumes more runway than exists is a hope.
- **Cash on hand is not always spendable.** Restricted cash, outstanding obligations, and minimum balances all reduce the real number.
- **See [bootstrapping](#bootstrapping)** — the alternative to raising is growing into your own runway.
entries.formula: Runway (months) = cash on hand / monthly burn rate
entries.how_to_read: Below six months you are fundraising whether you want to or not. Above eighteen months you have the luxury of choosing.

entries.title: Sales Cycle
entries.one_line_definition: The time from first meaningful contact with a buyer to a signed deal.
entries.why_it_matters: It determines your cash timing and your hiring plan. A longer cycle means more pipeline must exist at any moment to hit the same revenue.
entries.body:
Sales cycle is how long a deal takes to close. It is a structural property of your market — set by the buyer's process, the price, and the risk — not a performance metric you can simply improve.

Its importance is in the arithmetic it imposes. Revenue this quarter comes from pipeline created many months earlier, so the cycle length sets how far ahead you must be working.

## Worked example

A company closes $40,000 deals with a 90-day cycle. To close $400,000 in a quarter, it needs $400,000 of qualified pipeline created roughly 90 days earlier — about 10 deals in motion at all times.

Now the same company sells a $4,000 version with a 7-day cycle:

    400,000 / 4,000 = 100 deals
    But the pipeline only needs to exist 7 days ahead

The smaller deal needs far more volume but far less foresight, and it can be closed by a much less expensive seller. That is the core trade-off between a high-ACV and low-ACV motion.

## Watch for

- **Measure per segment.** A blended average across a self-serve and an enterprise motion describes neither.
- **The cycle has stages.** Knowing where time is spent — discovery, legal, procurement — tells you what to shorten.
- **Cycle length sets the payback of a hire.** A new salesperson on a 12-month cycle produces nothing for a year. Plan hiring ahead of revenue, not behind it.
entries.formula: Sales cycle = date closed - date of first qualified contact
entries.how_to_read: Read it per segment, not as one number. Enterprise and self-serve cycles differ by an order of magnitude and need different motions.

entries.title: Enterprise vs Self-serve
entries.one_line_definition: Choosing whether customers buy from a salesperson or directly from the product.
entries.why_it_matters: It determines your cost structure, your pricing ceiling, and your hiring plan. It is the most consequential go-to-market decision a company makes.
entries.body:
A sales motion uses people to close deals. A self-serve motion uses the product and pricing page. They are not two versions of the same thing — they are different businesses with different economics.

The decision is arithmetic. A salesperson costs money whether or not they sell. If a customer is not worth more than that cost, a salesperson cannot serve them profitably.

## Worked example

    Salesperson fully loaded:   $180,000/year
    Expected quota:              $450,000/year
    Implied cost of sale:        40% of revenue

    Self-serve ACV:              $1,200/year
    Cost to serve via sales:     $480  →  the sale is unprofitable

    Enterprise ACV:              $60,000/year
    Cost to serve via sales:     $24,000 →  gross margin 60%, viable

The same sales team is ruinous at $1,200 and reasonable at $60,000. That is why low-ACV products must be self-serve, and why enterprise products almost always need a seller.

## Watch for

- **The motions blur.** Selling enterprise while leaving a self-serve page creates two conflicting price lists and confuses both buyers.
- **A sales motion hides product problems.** If the product cannot sell itself, a sales team will paper over the gap until the cost of sale becomes unsustainable.
- **Switching motions is expensive.** Moving up-market means retraining, re-pricing, and usually rebuilding the product. Decide early.
entries.when_to_use: When deciding how to take a product to market, or when a motion stops working at a new price point.
entries.when_not_to_use: When the product has not yet found fit — a sales motion before fit is an expensive way to learn nothing.
steps: Estimate the value of one customer per year.
Estimate the cost of one salesperson per year.
Compare: does one seller's output justify their cost?
Choose the motion that matches the ratio, then build for it.
entries.limitations: Most companies end up with both, and the two motions compete for the same product and the same customers. Managing that conflict is the real work.

entries.title: Second-order Thinking
entries.one_line_definition: Asking what happens after the thing you decided, and after that, before concluding the decision is good.
entries.why_it_matters: Most bad decisions are good first-order decisions with unexamined consequences. The first-order effect is visible and the second-order one is not, which is exactly why it is missed.
entries.body:
Second-order thinking is the discipline of following a decision past its immediate effect. The immediate effect is usually obvious and often good; the next one is where the cost hides.

It is not about being cautious. It is about seeing the whole chain before committing, so that a decision that looks free is recognised as expensive.

## Worked example

A company cuts its support team from 10 to 6 to save $240,000 a year:

    First order:   payroll down $240,000. Obvious, measurable, immediate.
    Second order:  response time rises from 10 minutes to 45.
    Third order:   satisfaction falls; churn rises 2 points; at $200 ARR per customer and 5,000 customers, that is $200,000 a year lost.
    Net:           the saving cost $200,000 and bought a worse product.

The first-order view shows a $240,000 win. The full chain shows a $40,000 loss and a product that is harder to sell. Both are true; only one was examined.

## Watch for

- **Time is the mechanism.** Second-order effects arrive later, so they are never present at the moment of decision. You have to go looking for them.
- **Ask "and then what?" three times.** Most chains are short enough to trace, and the third question usually surfaces the real cost.
- **Not every second-order effect is negative.** Some decisions look expensive and pay back twice. The discipline works in both directions.
entries.statement: Every action has consequences, and those consequences have consequences. Judging the first and ignoring the second is how apparently obvious decisions fail.
entries.evidence: Cutting support staff reduces cost immediately and increases churn over two quarters. The first effect is measured and celebrated; the second arrives later and is attributed to something else.
entries.failure_mode: Optimising the visible metric in the current quarter because the cost of the decision lands in a later quarter someone else will own.

entries.title: Segmentation
entries.one_line_definition: Dividing the market into groups whose needs differ enough to warrant a different offer.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the mechanism that makes positioning possible. You cannot be for everyone, so you choose who to be for by segmenting first.
entries.body:
Segmentation is splitting a market into groups that want different things. It is the step between "who is our customer?" and "what do we build for them?"

The trap is segmenting by description instead of by need. Two companies in the same industry and of the same size may need entirely different things. Segmenting by what they are rather than what they need produces groups that cannot be served differently.

## Worked example

A bookkeeping tool's market splits by need:

    Segment A — freelancers: want speed and low price, buy alone, churn fast
    Segment B — 10-person agencies: want client management, buy for a team, churn slowly
    Segment C — 100-person firms: want compliance and integrations, buy through procurement, churn never

Same software, three different products in practice. Segment B values a feature A would never pay for and C would find trivial. Pricing, messaging, and roadmap all differ. Serving all three with one message produces a product that is mediocre for each.

## Watch for

- **Segments must be actionable.** If you cannot reach the group differently, it is not a segment — it is a description.
- **Start with one.** Serving two segments well beats serving four badly. Expand from a segment you own.
- **Segments change as you grow.** The segment that fits a ten-person company may be wrong at a hundred. Revisit it.
entries.how_to_read: Read segments by need and by behaviour, not by demographics. Age and job title are proxies; the need is the thing.

entries.title: 7 Powers
entries.one_line_definition: Seven distinct sources of durable advantage, each with a different mechanism and a different prerequisite.
entries.why_it_matters: It separates advantages that are real from those that merely feel real, by asking what must be true for the advantage to exist.
entries.body:
7 Powers categorises advantage into seven mechanisms: scale economies, network economies, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resource, and process power.

Its usefulness is precision. "We have a moat" is unfalsifiable; "we have switching costs because migrating our data format takes six months" is a claim you can test and an investor can check.

## Worked example

    Scale economies     — unit cost falls as volume rises. Prerequisite: a large addressable market and a cost curve that actually bends.
    Network economies  — value rises with users. Prerequisite: connections between customers.
    Counter-positioning — a new model incumbents cannot copy without harming themselves. Prerequisite: an incumbent with a business model that blocks the response.
    Switching costs    — leaving is expensive. Prerequisite: integration into the customer's operations.
    Branding           — a price premium from trust. Prerequisite: repeated purchase and uncertainty about quality.
    Cornered resource  — exclusive access to something scarce. Prerequisite: a resource others cannot obtain.
    Process power      — embedded know-how that improves with repetition. Prerequisite: a long, stable production history.

A SaaS tool with deep integrations holds switching costs. A search engine holds scale economies and network economies. Neither holds branding in any meaningful sense, and claiming it would be a category error.

## Watch for

- **A power requires its prerequisite.** Claiming network effects for a product with no connections between users is a category error, not a strategy.
- **Powers have half-lives.** Counter-positioning works only while the incumbent is constrained.
- **Pick one to build.** Attempting all seven spreads effort and usually produces none.
entries.when_to_use: When you need to articulate defensibility to an investor or decide which advantage to build toward.
entries.when_not_to_use: As a checklist to optimise against — the powers are alternative paths, not a scorecard.
steps: Identify which power your business could plausibly hold.
Check the prerequisite condition for that power.
Check whether the power is present at the time you enter the market.
Build the mechanism, not the claim.
entries.limitations: It is a taxonomy of advantage, not a method for creating it. Knowing the categories does not tell you which one your market will reward.

entries.title: The Term Sheet
entries.one_line_definition: The document setting out the terms on which an investor will put money into the company.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the contract that governs the relationship for years. Most of the value is not in the valuation — it is in the control and liquidation terms buried after it.
entries.body:
A term sheet is the agreement on price and terms before the legal documents. It is short, and the important clauses are the ones that decide what happens when things go badly.

Valuation gets the attention. But the clauses that matter most are control (board seats, protective provisions), liquidation preference (who gets paid first and how much), and option pool size.

## Worked example

Two offers for the same company:

    Offer A:  $3,000,000 at a $12,000,000 pre-money valuation
              1x non-participating preference, 2 board seats (1 investor)

    Offer B:  $3,000,000 at a $10,000,000 pre-money valuation
              2x participating preference, 3 board seats (2 investor), full ratchet

Offer A is better despite the higher valuation of Offer B being... no — Offer A has the higher valuation and cleaner terms. Offer B takes more control, guarantees the investor double their money before anyone else sees a return, and adjusts the price downward if a later round is raised lower. At a modest exit, Offer B can return more to the investor than the founders receive.

## Watch for

- **Liquidation preference changes everything at a low exit.** A 2x participating preference can take most of a small exit before founders see anything.
- **Protective provisions are control.** A veto over ordinary decisions is more restrictive than a board seat.
- **Read the anti-dilution clause.** A full ratchet punishes a down round far more severely than a weighted average, and it is the clause that destroys founder value.
entries.how_to_read: Read it for control and downside, not for the headline number. A higher valuation with worse terms is often worth less than a lower one with clean terms.

entries.title: Throughput
entries.one_line_definition: The rate at which a system produces what it is for, measured in units of value per unit of time.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the honest measure of capacity. A team busy at 100% utilisation often produces less than one at 70%, because there is no slack to absorb variation.
entries.body:
Throughput is how much a system delivers per unit of time. It applies to factories, support queues, and software teams alike, because all of them are systems with a limiting step.

The counter-intuitive part is that maximising individual utilisation reduces throughput. A station running at 100% has no capacity to absorb a surge, so work piles up in front of it and the whole system slows.

## Worked example

A support team handles tickets in three steps:

    Step         Capacity
    Triage       40 tickets/hour
    Resolution   12 tickets/hour
    Follow-up    30 tickets/hour

The system's throughput is 12 tickets/hour — the resolution step. Triage at 40 and follow-up at 30 are irrelevant to output; they are idle waiting for work.

Now triage is staffed to 100% utilisation. When a surge arrives, tickets queue, nothing reaches resolution faster, and the queue grows without any increase in completed work. The team feels busier and delivers less.

## Watch for

- **Throughput is set by the slowest step.** Improving any other step adds cost, not output.
- **Utilisation and throughput are different.** High utilisation with a queue is a warning sign, not a success.
- **Measure in value, not activity.** Tickets touched, commits merged, and meetings held are not throughput. Completed, usable work is.
entries.formula: Throughput = units of value completed per unit of time
entries.how_to_read: Read it as a rate, not a total. Two systems with the same output can have very different throughputs, and only one can grow.

entries.title: Value Creation Before Value Capture
entries.one_line_definition: A business exists to create value; capturing it is what makes the creation sustainable.
entries.why_it_matters: Almost every failed venture captured value it never created — a rent, a fee, a markup — and the market eventually noticed.
entries.body:
Business has two halves. **Value creation** is making something worth more than the sum of its parts — a product that saves time, a service that removes risk, a market that connects two sides. **Value capture** is keeping a share of that surplus as profit.

The order matters. Creation comes first, and capture follows as a consequence. The reverse — designing a capture mechanism and hoping value appears — is how you get a business model that works only while no one is looking.

## Worked example

A logistics startup connects truckers with shippers:

- Without it: a shipper pays $2,000 and waits two days to find a truck.
- With it: the shipper pays $1,600 and gets a truck in two hours.

The value created is roughly $400 in price plus the time saved. If the startup keeps $120 as its fee, it created $400 and captured $120. The surplus is real, so both sides return.

Now suppose the startup instead charged $450 while providing nothing the shipper could not do alone. It captures more than it creates. The moment a cheaper connector appears, it is gone — because there was nothing holding the customer there.

## Watch for

- **Capture without creation is a toll, not a business.** Tolls last exactly as long as the road is the only route.
- **Creating without capturing is a hobby.** Generous surplus with no margin runs out of money.
- **See [product-market-fit](#product-market-fit)** — the test for whether the value is real at all.
entries.statement: Create more value than you capture, and the capture becomes durable. Capture more than you create, and it becomes temporary.
entries.evidence: Companies with a genuine surplus to give — cheaper, faster, better — compound. Companies extracting a spread without adding anything are disintermediated the moment a cheaper route appears.
entries.failure_mode: Confusing revenue with value. A customer paying you is not proof you created value; it is proof you have not yet been replaced.
